text: Review The bile acid-gut microbiota axis: A central hub for physiological regulation and a novel therapeutic target for metabolic diseases Min Zhao , Jiafeng Zhao , Huimin Yang , Zirou Ouyang , Chang Lv , Zijun Geng , Jianhong Zhao * Hebei Provincial Center for Clinical Laboratories, The Second Hospital of Hebei Medical University, Shijiazhuang, Hebei, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Bile acid Enterohepatic circulation Gut microbiota Metabolic disease Treatment A B S T R A C T Bile acids are a family of signaling molecules synthesized in the liver and metabolized by gut bacteria. As me­ tabolites of the intestinal microbiota, bile acids bind to various receptors, and affect the metabolism and immune function of the host, including glucose and lipid metabolism, energy homeostasis, and inflammatory response. Conversely, bile acids also shape the composition of the gut microbiota. Given their critical role in physiological regulation, disrupted bile acid signaling is closely linked to metabolic diseases. Consequently, therapeutic strategies targeting bile acids are increasingly being explored. The size, composition, and function of the bile acid pool can be modulated through direct treatments (e.g., bile acid replacement therapy, administration of bile acid receptor agonists/antagonists) or indirect treatments (e.g., gut microbiota modulation, probiotic supplementa­ tion), providing new ideas for preventing and treating metabolic diseases. 1. Introduction The gut microbiota and its metabolites, particularly bile acids (BAs), play crucial roles in various physiological processes, including nutrient absorption, metabolic regulation, physiological homeostasis, and host immune defense. BAs, a group of steroidal acids, can be classified into primary and secondary BAs based on their origin. Primary BAs, syn­ thesized in the liver from cholesterol, include cholic acid (CA), cheno­ deoxycholic acid (CDCA), and their glycine or taurine conjugates. Upon entering the intestine, these primary BAs undergo microbial

nutrient absorption, metabolic regulation, physiological homeostasis, and host immune defense. BAs, a group of steroidal acids, can be classified into primary and secondary BAs based on their origin. Primary BAs, syn­ thesized in the liver from cholesterol, include cholic acid (CA), cheno­ deoxycholic acid (CDCA), and their glycine or taurine conjugates. Upon entering the intestine, these primary BAs undergo microbial trans­ formation into secondary BAs, such as deoxycholic acid (DCA) and lithocholic acid (LCA) [1]. These molecules modulate various host metabolic processes—including glucose and lipid metabolism, energy homeostasis, and inflammatory responses—by activating specific re­ ceptors in both hepatic and intestinal tissues. Recent advances in elucidating the intricate interplay between the gut microbiota and BAs have revealed that compositional and functional alterations in the gut microbial community can remarkably influence the metabolism and composition of BAs, thereby contributing to the pathogenesis and progression of metabolic disorders [2,3]. Environ­ mental perturbations that disrupt the gut microbiota or microbiota-host interactions can hinder the synthesis and metabolism of BAs. Dysregu­ lation of BA signaling is associated with various metabolic disorders, including obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and chole­ stasis [4,5]. Given the physiological and pathological significance of BA signaling, BA-targeted therapies have emerged as promising treatment approaches for metabolic disorders. These strategies include direct in­ terventions, such as BA replacement and administration of synthetic BA receptor agonists/antagonists, as well as indirect methods, such as fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) and probiotic supplementation. The present review systematically explores three critical aspects of BA biology: (1) the signaling pathways associated with BA metabolism, (2) the bidirectional interactions between BAs and the gut microbiota and their implications in metabolic disorders, and (3) emerging BA-targeted therapeutic strategies. By integrating these interconnected elements, our work provides a comprehensive framework for

The rate-limiting enzyme, cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7A1), initiates the conversion of cholesterol to 7α-hydroxycholesterol. This intermediate is subsequently metabolized by 3β-hydroxyΔ5-C27-steroid dehydrogenase (HSD3B7) to form 7α-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one (C4) [7]. As a pivotal metabolic intermediate, C4 serves dual roles: (1) as the primary precursor for the synthesis of both CA and CDCA, and (2) as a clinically relevant biomarker for assessing the synthesis rates of hepatic BAs. C4 is further converted into the CA precursor (3α,7α,12α-trihydroxycholestanoic acid) under the action of sterol 12α-hydroxylase (CYP8B1), aldo-keto reductase (Δ4–3-oxosteroid-5β-reductase), and sterol 27-hydroxylase (CYP27A1) or into the CDCA precursor (3α,7α-dihydroxycholestanoic acid) in the absence of 12α-hydroxylation. Primary BAs are conjugated with taurine or glycine via two enzymatic steps: BA-coenzyme A (CoA) synthetase and BA-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase, forming conju­ gated primary BAs. These conjugated BAs then enter the intestine, where bile salt hydrolases (BSHs) deconjugated them, follow by 7α-dehy­ droxylation mediated by the bile acid-inducible (bai) operon of gut microbiota to generate DCA and LCA [8,9]. Following liver damage or impairment of the classical synthesis pathway in patients with liver diseases, the alternative pathway be­ comes activated as the primary route for BA synthesis [10]. The alter­ native pathway is initiated by two distinct enzymatic reactions: (1) sterol 25-hydroxylase hydroxylates cholesterol to form 25-hydroxycho­ lesterol in the liver, and (2) CYP27A1 converts cholesterol into 3β-hydroxy-5-cholestenoic acid in hepatocytes, macrophages, and ad­ renal glands. Both compounds subsequently undergo oxysterol 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7B1)-mediated 7α-hydroxylation to yield 3β, 7α-dihydroxy-5-cholestenoic acid. This oxysterol is produced in extra­ hepatic tissues and transported to the liver, where it is converted into CDCA. This oxysterol is produced in extra­ hepatic tissues and transported to the liver, where it is converted into CDCA. Previous studies have demonstrated interspecies variation in CDCA conversion within liver microsomes among humans, mice, rats, dogs, and rabbits [8,9]. In mice, the majority of CDCA is rapidly con­ verted into the more hydrophilic α-muricholic acid (α-MCA) by ster­ ol-6β-hydroxylase. Subsequently, the 7α-hydroxy group of α-MCA undergoes 7α-β-isomerase-catalyzed epimerization to a 7β-hydroxy group, leading to the formation of β-MCA. In contrast, a portion of CDCA in humans is transformed into ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) through bacterial 7β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (7β-HSDH) [11]. 3. Enterohepatic circulation of BAs Conjugated primary BAs, characterized by their strong hydrophilic­ ity, are actively transported via the bile salt export pump (BSEP) and subsequently stored in the gallbladder [12]. Postprandial release of cholecystokinin from the pancreas stimulates the secretion of BAs into the intestinal lumen [13,14]. Approximately 95 % of conjugated BAs are actively absorbed by intestinal epithelial cells through the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT). Following absorption, these conjugated BAs bind to ileal bile acid-binding protein (IBABP) and traverse the basolateral membrane via the organic solute transporter alpha/beta (OSTα/OSTβ) complex, ultimately returning to the liver via the portal vein. These recycled BAs, along with newly synthesized BAs from the liver, are secreted into the bile and subsequently released into the intestine during feeding, thereby completing the enterohepatic Fig. 1. Gut microbiota-mediated regulation of BA metabolism During the enterohepatic circulation, microbial-synthesized enzymes play pivotal roles in BA transformation. This review focuses on BSHs, hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases (HSDHs), and the bai operon [9,16]. Table 1 summarizes the gut microbial species involved in BAs biosyn­ thesis and their primary enzymatic functions. 4.1.1. BSH catalyzes the deconjugation reaction Upon entering the intestine, conjugated BAs are hydrolyzed by microbiota-derived BSHs [17]. BSHs recognize and cleave the amide bond between BAs and glycine/taurine at their active sites, converting conjugated BAs into free forms (e.g., CA and CDCA) and corresponding amino acids (glycine or taurine), thus completing the deconjugation process [32,33]. Multiple bacterial genera, including Bacteroides, Clos­ tridium, Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Enterococcus, and Listeria, exhibit BSH activity [18,21,23,34]. These microbial species typically show enhanced bile tolerance and superior intestinal colonization capabilities [20]. The unconjugated BAs, characterized by their poor solubility, escape active absorption by small intestinal cells and transit to the colon, where they undergo further microbial metabolism to generate secondary BAs (e.g., DCA and LCA) [22]. Beyond deconjugation, BSHs also facili­ tates the formation of bacterial BA amides by catalyzing the conjugation of amines with BAs, thereby expanding the diversity of BAs [35,36]. 4.1.2. HSDH catalyzes both hydroxyl oxidation and epimerization reactions HSDH catalyzes the reversible oxidation of hydroxyl groups (-OH) to keto groups at specific positions (e.g., C-3, C-7, and C-12) of BAs [24, 25]. Subsequently, HSDH alters the stereochemical configuration of BA molecules through redox reactions by inducing epimerization of hy­ droxyl groups at specific carbon atoms, thereby modifying the spatial structure of BAs

both hydroxyl oxidation and epimerization reactions HSDH catalyzes the reversible oxidation of hydroxyl groups (-OH) to keto groups at specific positions (e.g., C-3, C-7, and C-12) of BAs [24, 25]. Subsequently, HSDH alters the stereochemical configuration of BA molecules through redox reactions by inducing epimerization of hy­ droxyl groups at specific carbon atoms, thereby modifying the spatial structure of BAs [37]. Epimerization requires the coordinated action of two position-specific HSDHs (e.g., α- and β-HSDHs) [26]. For instance, 3α-HSDH, 7α-HSDH, or 12α-HSDH first oxidize hydroxyl groups to keto groups (e.g., 3-, 7-, 12-keto BAs), followed by reduction of these keto groups to β-hydroxyl groups by 3β-HSDH, 7β-HSDH, or 12β-HSDH, respectively [27]. Multiple gut bacteria species, including Bacteroides, Clostridium, and Eubacterium species, can independently or synergisti­ cally participate in this process [20,25,30]. The bai operon catalyzes the dehydroxylation reaction The bai operon is a gene cluster encoding multiple enzymes, including BaiB, BaiCD, BaiA2, BaiE, BaiF, BaiG, BaiH, and BaiI, which collectively catalyze BA dehydroxylation [24]. Initially, BaiB, func­ tioning as a bile acid-CoA ligase, catalyzes the adenylation of BAs to form cholyl-coenzyme A (cholyl-CoA), representing a critical step in the overall reaction cascade [30]. Subsequently, BaiA2 catalyzes 3-dehy­ droxylation of cholyl-CoA to generate 3-oxo-cholyl-CoA, which is further oxidized by BaiCD to form 3-oxo-4,5-dehydro-cholyl-CoA [34]. Next, BaiE catalyzes the critical step of 7α-dehydroxylation to form 3-oxo-Δ4,5–6,7-deoxycholyl-CoA [37]. During the reduction phase, BaiH removes the CoA moiety. Two sequential oxidation steps mediated by BaiCD and BaiA2, ultimately yielding DCA or other secondary BAs [38]. Firmicutes genera, including Clostridium and Eubacterium, utilize the bai operon to mediate 7α-dehydroxylation, converting CA and CDCA into DCA and LCA, respectively [20,37]. 4.2. BAs modulate gut microbiota composition A bidirectional regulatory relationship exists between the gut microbiota and BAs. On the one hand, the gut microbiota modulates the metabolism of BAs, influencing the size and composition of the BA pool [9]. On the other hand, via their unique chemical properties and phys­ iological functions, BAs selectively promote or inhibit the growth of specific microbial populations, thereby reshaping gut microbiota composition [22]. The following sections detail the regulatory effects of BAs on the gut microbiota. 4.2.1. Direct antimicrobial activity of BAs BAs can act as antimicrobial agents by disrupting cell membranes or altering intracellular macromolecular structures [39]. At low concen­ trations, BAs modulate membrane permeability and hydrophobicity through interactions with microbial surface proteins, whereas at high concentrations, they rapidly degrade membrane proteins in microbial cells [40]. Therefore, only those

of BAs on the gut microbiota. 4.2.1. Direct antimicrobial activity of BAs BAs can act as antimicrobial agents by disrupting cell membranes or altering intracellular macromolecular structures [39]. At low concen­ trations, BAs modulate membrane permeability and hydrophobicity through interactions with microbial surface proteins, whereas at high concentrations, they rapidly degrade membrane proteins in microbial cells [40]. Therefore, only those microbial communities that can tolerate high concentrations of BAs survive in the intestinal environment. Pre­ vious research indicates that different types of BAs exhibit remarkable inhibitory effects on specific pathogens. For instance, DCA inhibits the growth of Clostridioides difficile, while UDCA directly suppresses the germination of C. difficile spores in vitro [41]. Additionally, iso-LCA demonstrates substantial antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive multidrug-resistant pathogens, such as Enterococcus faecium [26]. San­ nasiddappa et al. [42] revealed that BAs exert antibacterial effects on Staphylococcus aureus at different concentrations through distinct mechanisms. At the minimum inhibitory concentration, BAs achieve bactericidal effects by disrupting the bacterial cell membrane, leading to the leakage of cellular contents [40]. In contrast, at subinhibitory con­ centrations, BAs inhibit bacterial growth by impairing the proton motive force in bacterial cells, thereby disrupting the transmembrane potential and increasing membrane permeability. Notably, unconjugated BAs passively penetrate bacterial cell membranes via the “flip-flop” mecha­ nism, with their efficiency affected by the number of hydroxyl groups in the BA molecules: the fewer hydroxyl groups, the greater the penetration ability [40]. Moreover, unconjugated BAs exhibit stronger antimicrobial activity compared to their conjugated counterparts [42,43]. 4.2.2. BA-mediated regulation of gut microbiota structure Studies have shown that supplemental BAs can alter gut microbiota composition [9]. Obeticholic acid (OCA), a derivative of CDCA, inhibits endogenous BA synthesis and increases the abundance of Gram-positive bacteria such as Streptococcus thermophilus, Lactobacillus casei, Lactoba­ cillus paracasei, Bifidobacterium breve, and Lactococcus lactis, while reducing the abundance of Gram-negative bacteria [44]. Chen et al. [45] utilized the db/db mice model for assessing the effects of BAs on obesity and T2DM; the authors found that the administration of glyco­ ursodeoxycholic acid (GUDCA) effectively mitigated the onset and progression of diabetes. Additionally, the abundance of Bacteroides vul­ gatus in the intestines of db/db mice was significantly increased [46]. Similarly, supplementation with DCA also induces significant alterations in gut microbiota composition. DCA administration promotes the growth of Akkermansia muciniphila in the intestines of mice [46]. 4.2.3. FXR activation-dependent indirect modulation of the gut microbiota by BAs In addition to direct regulation, BAs can indirectly modulate gut microbiota composition by activating specific receptors such as the farnesoid X receptor (FXR) [15]. FXR activation upregulates the expression of genes related to small intestinal mucosal defense, such as nitric oxide synthase and interleukin-18, thereby promoting the syn­ thesis of antimicrobial molecules such as nitric oxide and inhibiting bacterial growth [47]. 5. Physiological regulation of BAs and their receptor functions BAs function as critical signaling molecules by binding to various receptors, including the FXR [48], Takeda G-protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5) [45], vitamin D receptor [49], and pregnane X receptor [50], thereby modulating downstream cellular signaling pathways. The investigation of the expression and functional changes of BAs and their receptors in metabolic diseases provides critical insights into the pathogenesis of these conditions. This review focuses on the roles of FXR and TGR5

This review focuses on the roles of FXR and TGR5 in the synthesis and metabolism of BAs (Fig. 3) and futher discusses how these regulatory processes influence systemic glucose and lipid metabolism (Fig. 4), energy homeostasis, and inflammatory re­ sponses (Fig. 5). 5.1. Regulation of FXR and TGR5 in BA homeostasis and metabolic synthesis 5.1.1. FXR FXR is expressed in multiple organs, including the liver, intestine, kidneys, white adipose tissue, and immune cells [51], with the highest expression levels observed in the liver and intestine. As the primary receptor for BAs, FXR plays a pivotal role in regulating the synthesis, transport, and metabolism of BAs [52]. Primary BAs (CA and CDCA) and secondary BAs (DCA and LCA) act as activators of FXR, and their acti­ vation efficacy follows the order: CDCA > DCA > CA > LCA [53]. In contrast, T-αMCA and T-βMCA function as intestinal FXR antagonists [54]. Following activation by BAs, hepatic FXR induces the expression of the small heterodimer partner (SHP). SHP synergizes with hepatocyte nuclear factor-4α (HNF-4α) and liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1) to suppress the expression of key enzymes in BA biosynthesis, including cyp7a1 and cyp8b1 [55]. This process promotes the efficient excretion of BAs. In the intestine, BAs activate FXR, inducing the production of fibroblast growth factor 15/19 (FGF15/19). This signaling molecule is then transported to the liver, where it specifically binds to fibroblast growth factor receptor 4 (FGFR4) and β-klotho. In the intestine, FXR promotes the transport of BAs to the sinusoidal membrane by inhibiting ASBT expression and enhancing IBABP expression. TGR5 TGR5 is a membrane-bound receptor widely distributed in the liver, intestine, pancreas, central nervous system, and immune cells [58]. BAs show varying efficacy in activating TGR5, with the potency in the following order: LCA > DCA > CDCA > CA [59]. TGR5 activation downregulates cyp8b1 expression, leading to a decrease in the ratio of 12α-hydroxylated BAs (12α-OH BAs) to non-12α-hydroxylated BAs (non-12α-OH BAs) in the BA pool [60]. Additionally, TGR5 enhances the efficiency of the synthesis and metabolism of BAs by activating other enzymes in the alternative pathway, such as CYP7B1 and CYP27A1 [61]. 5.2. Role of BAs in regulating blood glucose levels As crucial bioactive molecules, BAs actively participate in the regu­ lation of blood glucose homeostasis by effectively inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis, promoting glycogen synthesis, and enhancing insulin sensitivity, thereby maintaining glucose stability. In the liver, the acti­ vated FXR induces SHP expression. SHP subsequently suppresses key gluconeogenic enzymes, such as phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase), and glucose-6- phosphatase (G6Pase), through SHP-dependent interactions with HNF- 4 [62] and forkhead transcription factor (FOXO1) [63], thereby inhib­ iting hepatic gluconeogenesis [64–66]. FXR also promotes hepatic glycogen synthesis by activating the PI3K/AKT/GSK3β signaling cascade, which upregulates the expression of glycogen synthase [67]. Additionally, FXR enhances the function of glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2), which facilitates the transport of blood glucose into hepato­ cytes, stimulating insulin production and secretion [68]. Additionally, FXR enhances the function of glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2), which facilitates the transport of blood glucose into hepato­ cytes, stimulating insulin production and secretion [68]. Intestinal FXR induces the production of FGF15/19, which, following transportation to the liver, binds to the FGFR4/β-klotho complex. This process, indepen­ dent of insulin signaling, directly promotes hepatic glycogen synthesis and suppresses gluconeogenesis [69]. Moreover, intestinal BAs activate TGR5, stimulating the secretion of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) [70]. GLP-1 regulates glucose metabolism and energy balance by promoting insulin production, inhibiting gastric emptying and acid secretion, delaying intestinal motility, enhancing satiety, and reducing food intake [71,72]. 5.3. Role of BAs in regulating lipid metabolism BAs play a crucial role in regulating lipid metabolism and main­ taining lipid homeostasis. On the one hand, BAs promote fat emulsifi­ cation by binding to lipids and disintegrating them into smaller particles [73]. BAs increase the contact area between fats and lipases, which accelerates lipid digestion and absorption. BAs also bind to cholesterol transport proteins in the intestine, which facilitates cholesterol excretion and reduces its reabsorption [74]. On the other hand, BAs activate re­ ceptors, particularly FXR, and regulate downstream pathways, thereby achieving precise control over lipid metabolism [75]. Following the binding of BAs to FXR, the activated FXR induces SHP expression, which suppresses the transcription of the sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1c (SREBP-1c). This further downregulates the activity of key lipogenic enzymes, such as fatty acid synthetase (FAS), acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), and stearoyl-CoA desaturase-1 (SCD-1), thereby reducing hepatic triglyceride levels [76,77]. FXR activation upregulates syndecan-1[79], apolipo­ protein C-II (ApoC-II) [80], and apolipoprotein A-V (ApoA-V) [81]. Conversely, it suppresses microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) [82], apolipoprotein B (ApoB) [82], and apolipoprotein C-III (ApoC-III) [83], reducing hepatic VLDL and chylomicron levels. This mechanism contributes to the stabilization of plasma cholesterol levels and facili­ tates hyperlipidemia prevention. 5.4. Role of BAs in regulating energy metabolism BAs modulate the expression of energy metabolism-related genes through receptor binding. In the intestine, TGR5 activation stimulates the cAMP-dependent thyroid hormone-activating enzyme deiodinase-2 (DIO2), which converts inactive thyroxine (T4) into active triiodothy­ ronine (T3) [84]. Activated T3 enhances mitochondrial oxygen con­ sumption and energy expenditure in murine brown adipocytes and human skeletal muscle cells. In muscle and brown adipose tissue, acti­ vated TGR5 prevents obesity and its complications by enhancing insulin sensitivity and promoting energy expenditure. Additionally, intestinal FXR enhances fatty acid β-oxidation and white adipose tissue browning by inducing the expression of proteins such as peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1α/β (PGC1α and PGC1β) [85] and uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) [86]. 5.5. Role of BAs in modulating inflammatory responses Following their entry into the intestine, liver-secreted BAs are con­ verted by gut microbiota from primary BAs to secondary BAs, which participate in the regulation of immune cell differentiation and subsequently modulate inflammatory responses [87]. Certain secondary BAs, such as 3-oxo-LCA and iso-LCA, regulate immune cell balance by promoting Treg cell differentiation and inhibiting Th17 cell differenti­ ation, thereby enhancing the anti-inflammatory capacity of the immune system [88,89]. This balance is crucial for maintaining organismal health, resisting pathogen infections, and preventing the onset of auto­ immune diseases. Additionally, BAs-activated cAMP signaling inhibits the NF-κB pathway, thereby suppressing the expression of lipopolysac­ charide (LPS)-induced inflammatory cytokines [90]. FXR and TGR5

Additionally, BAs-activated cAMP signaling inhibits the NF-κB pathway, thereby suppressing the expression of lipopolysac­ charide (LPS)-induced inflammatory cytokines [90]. FXR and TGR5 are expressed in various immune cells, this expression may contribute to their anti-inflammatory effects [91]. A previous study demonstrates that TGR5 suppresses LPS-induced chemokine expression via the AKT-mTOR-LIP pathway, thereby ameliorating obesity-induced insulin resistance and inflammatory responses [92]. 6. Regulatory mechanisms mediated by the BA-gut microbiota axis in metabolic diseases The pathogenesis of abnormal metabolic conditions, such as obesity, T2DM, NAFLD, IBD, and cholestasis, is frequently associated with metabolic dysregulation. These conditions are characterized by chronic low-grade inflammation, marked by the recruitment of immune- inflammatory cells and abnormal production of cytokines and acute- phase reactants. Some researchers have defined these disorders as “meta-inflammatory disorders” [93,94]. Given the crucial role of BAs in regulating glucose and lipid metabolism and maintaining systemic en­ ergy homeostasis, it is increasingly recognized that abnormal alterations in BA levels and composition may serve as crucial driving factors in the pathogenesis of these metabolic disorders. Obesity and T2DM T2DM is one of the leading causes of mortality and disability worldwide. According to previous studies, 49.6 % of the increase in T2DM prevalence is attributable to obesity trends [95]. In obese in­ dividuals, the abundance or increased number of adipocytes reduce in­ sulin receptor density on cell membranes, leading to insulin resistance. As insulin resistance progresses, it ultimately leads to the development of diabetes. Patients with obesity and insulin resistance show increased synthesis of BAs, particularly elevated serum levels of 12α-OH BAs (including CA and its derivatives) and significantly reduced levels of non-12α-OH BAs (including CDCA and its derivatives) [96]. A previous study demon­ strated that mice lacking the CYP8B1 enzyme (cyp8b1-/-) cannot syn­ thesize CA and exhibit increased production of CDCA. These mice were resistant to high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity and showed improved insulin sensitivity [97]. cyp8b1-/- mice also exhibited elevated levels of T-MCA, an intestinal FXR antagonist, which reduced FGF15 production and thereby influenced the synthesis and metabolism of BAs. Conversely, overexpression of the cyp8b1 gene in mice exacerbates metabolic issues such as SREBP-1c-mediated lipogenesis, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance [98]. The aforementioned studies demonstrate that CYP8B1 regulates the proportion of 12α-OH BAs within the BA pool, determining whether the metabolic end products are CA or CDCA. Alterations in the proportion of 12α-OH BAs can significantly reshape gut microbiota composition and play a crucial role in systemic metabolic regulation [99]. NAFLD NAFLD includes a spectrum of diseases characterized by inflamma­ tion and hepatocyte injury, ranging from simple hepatic steatosis to progressive nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), liver fibrosis, and potentially advancing to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma [104]. NAFLD often coexists with other metabolic disorders such as obesity, T2DM, and cardiovascular diseases, thereby increasing the risk of adverse clinical outcomes [105]. Cholestasis Cholestasis is characterized by impaired bile flow, leading to exces­ sive accumulation of BAs in the liver, reduced levels of intestinal BAs, and increased levels of systemic BAs. The accumulated BAs cause he­ patocyte and biliary damage as well as inflammation. Over time, chronic cholestasis can progress to liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, and ultimately result in liver failure or hepatocellular carcinoma [121]. In patients with cholestasis, the expression of hepatobiliary transport proteins is upre­ gulated, which reduces the uptake and synthesis of BAs and promotes their excretion, thereby limiting the accumulation of potentially toxic substances [122]. The adaptive regulatory mechanisms exhibited by the body under pathological conditions are mediated by multiple nuclear receptors, such as FXR and PXR, and intestinal hormones such as FGF-19. Activated FXR suppresses cyp7a1 expression to reduce BA synthesis and inhibits NTCP and OATP activity to decrease hepatic BA uptake, thereby preventing BA accumulation within hepatocytes [122]. A recent study by Song et al. [123] revealed that hepatic fgf4 is a direct target gene of FXR, which downregulates the transcription of cyp7a1 and cyp8b1 through paracrine signaling pathways. FXR-FGF4 controls BA synthesis and maintains BA pool homeostasis by acti­ vating the FGFR4-LRH-1 pathway. In cholestasis patients, hepatic FXR and FGF4 expression levels are reduced, which impairs the FXR-FGF4 signaling axis. Compared to wild-type mice, fgf4-deficient mice showed increased levels of BAs in the liver and intestine, resulting in the exacerbation of cholestasis and liver injury symptoms. Conversely, the administration of an FGF4 analog to mice suppresses BA synthesis and alleviates histopathological damage, such as necrosis and biliary fibrosis. In addition to affecting homeostasis of the BA pool, cholestasis also causes long-term effects on the intestinal flora. A previous study showed that BA stasis and liver injury typically recovered within a short period in a mouse model of hepatic cholestasis induced by temporary complete bile duct obstruction. FMT With an improved understanding of the role of the gut microbiota in diseases, restoring gut microbiota homeostasis to alleviate disease symptoms has emerged as a promising research field, with the treatment of recurrent C. difficile infection as a widely applied area [143]. FMT, an effective approach for alleviating gut microbiota dysbiosis, has been utilized for treating and preventing various metabolic diseases. Alle­ gretti et al. Another clinical study showed that FMT enhanced BA meta­ bolism by gut bacteria and delayed the progression of glucose tolerance impairment. Obese patients with FMT showed substantial improvements in blood glucose levels and insulin resistance, suggesting that FMT may help prevent metabolic syndrome [128]. Targeting BA receptors: agonists/antagonists 7.2.1. Receptor agonists OCA, a potent FXR agonist, shows remarkable potential in treating metabolic diseases by regulating the synthesis and transport of BAs. Currently, OCA is primarily used to treat primary biliary cholangitis by inhibiting BA synthesis, improving liver function, and reducing inflammation to alleviate the disease. Additionally, OCA promotes the growth of Firmicutes and shows significant efficacy in alleviating NASH [132]. In a multicenter clinical trial, NASH patients in the OCA treat­ ment group showed significant improvements in liver fibrosis [133]. Phase III clinical trials further demonstrated that OCA increases insulin sensitivity, improves the severity of T2DM, and significantly reduces hepatic steatosis and fibrosis [134]. However, this drug may cause se­ vere pruritus, and its long-term benefits and safety require further validation. A 12-week Phase IIa clinical trial revealed that MET-409, a non-BA, structurally optimized FXR agonist, significantly reduced liver fat con­ tent. However, at an oral dose of 50 mg/day, some patients experienced transient alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevation, along with side ef­ fects such as pruritus and increased low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [135]. Another study evaluated the safety and efficacy of the nonste­ roidal agonist Cilofexor (formerly GS-9674) in 140 NASH patients. Summary and outlook As signaling molecules, BAs interact with the host via receptors such as FXR and TGR5, participating in the regulation of glucose and lipid metabolism, energy balance, and immune-inflammatory responses. Within the enterohepatic circulation, gut microbiota and BAs mutually regulate each other. Dysregulation of this crosstalk, leading to microbial dysbiosis and altered bile acid homeostasis, may collectively contribute to the pathogenesis of various metabolic disorders, including obesity, T2DM, NAFLD, IBD, and cholestasis. Animal studies and clinical in­ vestigations have identified several potential therapeutic targets along the gut microbiota-BA-BA receptor signaling axis. Potential therapeutic interventions include: direct BAs supplementation (e.g., UDCA), phar­ macological modulation of BA transporters (e.g., ASBT inhibitors) and receptors (e.g., FXR agonists, TGR5 antagonists), gut microbiota mod­ ulation through FMT and targeted probiotic administration. However, developing effective and safe BA signaling-based therapies requires additional fundamental and translational research to address several key challenges: (1) significant differences exist between animal models and humans in BA pool composition and gut microbiota profiles. Given the instability of results from animal studies, caution should be exercised when extrapolating mouse model data to clinical applications. Researchers should prioritize using organoid models for preclinical testing, (2) substantial interindividual variations in BA metabolism and gut microbiota necessitate further investigation into personalized treatment approaches, (3) the dynamic interplay between microbiota and BAs requires deeper mechanistic exploration to facilitate the development of targeted probiotic and prebiotic interventions, (4) while current BA-targeted therapies have shown promise, most studies have been limited to short-term efficacy assessments. Additionally, treatment-associated pruritus remains a significant clinical challenge. Therefore, comprehensive evaluation of long-term safety and efficacy profiles is urgently needed, along with the development of more selec­ tive and safer bile acid receptor agonists/antagonists, and (5) precise quantification of BA levels in humans poses another challenge for BA therapy. In summary, the significance of BAs in physiology and pathology offers new opportunities for treating metabolic diseases. Further research is essential to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of BAs in metabolic disorders, which could provide novel insights for preventing and treating these conditions. Considering mucosal adaptive immunity from a holobiont perspective, where the host and its microbiome form a single physiological unit, emphasises the challenge of avoiding damaging responses to self-antigen and symbiotic microbial communities in the gut while protecting against potential pathogens. Intestinal tolerance mechanisms prevent maladaptive T and B cell responses to microbial, environmental, and self-antigens, which drive inflammation. We discuss the spectrum of antimicrobial and autoantibody responses and highlight mechanisms by which common IBD- associated adaptive immune responses contribute to disease. Introduction Autoimmunity in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has been recognised for over 60 years since the first IBD-as­ sociated autoantibodies were detected against colon extract in 1959 [1], but views on its contribution to the patho­ genesis of IBD have evolved over time. Today IBD is considered a complex immune-mediated inflammatory disease characterised by defective mucosal barrier function and excess pro-inflammatory innate and adaptive immune responses to a dysbiotic microbiome [2,3].

Today IBD is considered a complex immune-mediated inflammatory disease characterised by defective mucosal barrier function and excess pro-inflammatory innate and adaptive immune responses to a dysbiotic microbiome [2,3]. We consider mucosal adaptive immunity from a holo­ biont perspective, in which the host and its highly as­ sociated co-developing microbial communities are viewed as a single physiological unit. This shift in per­ spective emphasises that maintenance of tolerance to both self-antigen and the symbiotic microbiota is critical for mucosal homeostasis. It positions loss of tolerance as an important checkpoint in the development of IBD. We review the roles of the mucosal adaptive immune system in health and highlight mechanisms that provide host-protective immunity and maintain tolerance. We delineate how innate (auto)inflammatory processes and specific T and B cell defects contribute to loss of toler­ ance. Reviewing evidence from inborn errors of im­ munity (IEI) and mouse models, we show that autoimmune and inappropriate antimicrobial adaptive immune responses arise from defects in overlapping mucosal tolerance and immunoregulatory systems. We consider autoimmunity as part of a larger group of IBD- associated mucosal adaptive responses. We discuss how these responses can be bystander reactions with utility as biomarkers or can contribute to disease pathogenesis and present new therapeutic targets. homeostasis in the holobiont The intestinal microbiome is a complex community of organisms that exists in symbiosis with its host. Microbiota perform essential digestive, metabolic, and immunomodulatory functions in health, and disturbance of the microbiota can contribute to disease [4]. The close, mutually dependent relationship between host and its microbiome has led to the two being considered together as a single physiological unit, a holobiont [5]. This perspective highlights the challenge posed to the immune system at mucosal sites. Symbiotic microbial communities are part of the ‘holobiont-self’ and must be maintained, yet the intestinal lumen is not an im­ munologically privileged site. The mucosa is an active interface, where the immune system must support and contain beneficial luminal microbiota while protecting against pathogenic bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites. Maintaining homeostasis at this mucosal interface is complex. The epithelial barrier and innate immune system play an important role [2]. In this review of auto­ immunity in IBD, we focus on antigen-reactive re­ sponses of the adaptive immune system. Adaptive immunity influences the composition of microbial com­ munities, supports barrier function, and employs im­ munoregulatory effector functions to promote tolerance. The mucosal adaptive immune system — host- protective immunity and immune homeostasis In the intestinal lumen and mucus layer, microbial communities are influenced by secretory IgA produced by intestinal plasma cells in the lamina propria (LP). IgA affects luminal microbiota through immune exclusion, neutralisation of virulence factors, agglutination, and enchainment [8]. This limits bacterial translocation [9] and creates ecological niches for symbiotic bacteria [10] and fungi [11] by altering colonisation topography and targeting competing pathobionts. In the outermost layer of the gastrointestinal mucosa, in­ traepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) contribute to host pro­ tection and immune homeostasis. IELs comprise tissue- resident memory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (TRM cells) and unconventional T cells. Multiple regionally distinct TRM populations provide rapid, antigen-specific responses against intestinal pathogens [12]. Functional specialisation of these responses can be determined by the tissue niche, for example, small intestinal CD8+ TRM cells in the upper villus provide effector responses, while those in the lower villus contribute to a memory response [13]. Unconven­ tional T cells have atypical T cell receptors (TCRs) with reduced diversity, enabling rapid responses to a limited pool of antigens. Mucosa-associated invariant T (MAIT) and natural killer T (NKT) cells possess αβ-TCRs, which recognise microbial antigens from riboflavin biosynthesis presented on MR1, and lipids presented on CD1d, re­ spectively [14]. The γδ-TCR directly recognises microbial and host-derived ligands without major histocompatibility complex (MHC) antigen presentation. γδ-T cells alter the small intestine microbiome through faecal micro-RNA se­ cretion [15] and present antigen to CD4+ T cells influ­ encing their polarisation [16]. Single-cell analysis of the intraepithelial compartment reveals extensive functional heterogeneity, encompassing direct cytotoxicity against infected cells and pathogens, production of pro-in­ flammatory and barrier-supporting cytokines, antigen pre­ sentation, and tissue repair [12,17]. In the LP, CD4+ T cells also support mucosal barrier function. Th17 cells produce IL17A, IL17F, and IL22, which stimulate intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) to maintain tight junctions and produce antimicrobial peptides [18]. Pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as in­ terferon gamma (IFNy), tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimu­ lating factor (GM-CSF), produced by Th1 and some Th17 cells, recruit and activate innate immune cells to clear invasive organisms [19]. In addition to TCR- mediated Th1/Th17 effector functions, an abundant population of microbiota-reactive CD4+ CD161High T cells (CD4/CD8 double negative in mice) contribute to immune homeostasis through TCR-independent re­ sponses to cytokine stimulation and by TCR-dependent tissue repair activity [20]. IgA and an effective mucosal barrier contain microbiota and limit antigen exposure. This combines with specific immunoregulatory tolerance mechanisms to maintain homeostasis. to maintain homeostasis. Section 2: Tolerance and immune regulation in the intestinal mucosa FOXP3+ Tregs have a key role in maintaining tolerance to the microbiota and self-antigen [21]. Tregs can dif­ ferentiate in the thymus (tTregs) in response to high- affinity interaction with self-antigen on thymic antigen presenting cells (APCs) (e.g. AIRE-expressing medullary thymic-epithelial cells), so have a TCR repertoire en­ riched for self-antigen. Highly autoreactive thymic T cells can alternatively undergo clonal deletion, reducing the pool of self-reactive naïve effector T cells in the periphery [19]. Microbial antigen can be trafficked to the thymus by specialised APCs, which support education of microbiota-responsive effector T cells; it is not yet known whether they contribute to generation of micro­ biota-responsive tTregs [22]. Tregs are also generated in the periphery (pTregs) in response to specific microbiota such as Clostridia strains and Helicobacter hepaticus [19,23]. Helicobacter-specific pTreg differentiation is supported by specialised RORγt + APCs in mesenteric lymph nodes (mLN), which ex­ press the transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) acti­ vating integrin αvβ8 [24]. In intestinal lymphoid tissue, circulating tTregs and locally differentiated pTregs up­ regulate GPR15, CCR9, and α4β7 in response to the intestinal milieu, enabling migration to the LP [21]. Intestinal Tregs then form a distinct population, with prolonged tissue residency, preferential gut homing, and unique TCR repertoires [25]. Within the intestine, pTregs and tTregs have common functionality and are not separated by unbiased clustering of single-cell RNA-sequencing data [23,26]. They are maintained and proliferate in an LP micro-niche, sup­ ported by interactions with CD206+ macrophages, IL1B+ macrophages, and CD103+ dendritic cells [26]. They have multiple tolerogenic effector functions, including production of immunoregulatory cytokines (TGF-β, in­ terleukin [IL]-10, and IL35), expression of co-inhibitory 2 Autoimmunity www.sciencedirect.com Current Opinion in Immunology 2025, 94:102557

Im­ munoregulatory functions are also performed con­ stitutively by CD4+ FOXP3- type-1 regulatory T (Tr1) cells [19] and can be induced transiently in otherwise inflammatory CD4+ effector T cells [27]. Loss of tolerance due to regulatory T cell defects Loss of tolerance can occur due to defects in Treg dif­ ferentiation or effector functions or because mucosal immune homeostasis is disturbed (e.g. by epithelial or innate defects). Monogenic IEI can disrupt these pro­ cesses, enabling identification of nonredundant toler­ ance mechanisms in the intestine and assessment of how they relate to IBD (Table 1). Defective Treg differentiation occurs secondary to loss- of-function variants in FOXP3 or the IL2 signalling pathway (IPEX and IPEX-like syndrome). These syn­ dromes cause severe autoimmune enteropathy, often most severe in the small bowel and accompanied by anti- enterocyte autoantibody production [28,29]. Entero­ pathy in these conditions is evident in utero, and FOXP3-/- mice develop intestinal pathology in germ-free conditions, confirming defective tolerance to self-an­ tigen is the dominant pathogenic mechanism in global Treg deficiency [30,31]. However, IL2-/- mice that lack Tregs develop a microbiota-dependent colitis alongside systemic autoimmunity [32], indicating co-existing loss of tolerance to microbiota and autoimmunity. This may be particularly significant in a subgroup of patients with late-onset or atypical IPEX, who can develop IBD-like inflammation [29]. Loss-of-function variants in AIRE disrupt central toler­ ance mechanisms, resulting in autoreactive naïve ef­ fector T cells and impaired tTreg development. This results in widespread autoimmunity (APECED syn­ drome) frequently including autoimmune enteropathy (typically not IBD) [33]. The disease is characterised by autoantibodies against enterochromaffin cells [33] and mucosal-protective cytokines IL17A, IL17F, and IL22, which can cause chronic mucosal candidiasis [34]. Tregs employ several immunoregulatory effector func­ tions to promote tolerance (Figure 1). The best char­ acterised are direct cell-mediated inhibition by the co- inhibitory receptor CTLA-4 and production of IL-10. CTLA-4 is expressed by Tregs constitutively and con­ ventional T cells following activation. It binds and downregulates CD80 and CD86 on APCs, preventing activation of the co-stimulatory CD28 receptor [19]. CTLA-4 haploinsufficiency or deficiency of LRBA (re­ quired for CTLA-4 membrane recycling) cause an auto­ immune enteropathy resembling IPEX [28]. Inhibition of CTLA-4 in cancer immunotherapy induces autoimmune complications and an IBD-like colitis, which can be modulated by antibiotics and faecal microbial transplant [35]. Similarly, in murine colitis transfer models, blocking CTLA-4 on Tregs abrogates their suppressive ability [36], suggesting Treg CTLA-4 promotes tolerance to the mi­ crobiota as well as self-antigen. Genome-wide association studies implicate common genetic variants with subtle effects on Treg differentia­ tion and function with increased risk of IBD [37]. Defective epithelial and phagocytic barrier function drives adaptive immune responses Intestinal monocytes and macrophages are the key IL- 10-responsive cells in the intestinal mucosa. They have constitutive high surface expression of IL10R, defi­ ciency of which reproduces the phenotype of global IL10 deficiency [43]. IL10 signalling induces a meta­ bolic shift towards oxidative phosphorylation, associated with reduced production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reduced antigen presentation, and increased intracellular bactericidal activity [38]. These effects are counter­ balanced by microbial stimulation; lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation promotes glycolytic metabolism and pro-inflammatory cytokine production [38], while ex­ posure of normal monocytes to whole bacteria induces a state of acquired IL-10 resistance [44]. Defects in epithelial barrier function and phagocytic function increase microbial exposure, thereby coun­ tering the effect of IL10 and inducing loss of tolerance to the microbiota. Consistent with this concept is the finding that patients with chronic granulomatous disease (CGD), a monogenic IBD that disrupts innate in­ tracellular killing of bacteria, have high antimicrobial antibody titres even in the absence of intestinal in­ flammation [45]. Similarly, IBD patients with variants in NOD2 or IRGM [46], and with NFkB1 haplotypes [47] that impair microbial handling have higher titres of an­ timicrobial antibodies. Disrupting the IL10 axis, through genetic defect or by functionally offsetting the effects of IL10 signalling through microbial stimulation, results in loss of tolerance to the microbiota and IBD. Systemic autoimmunity is uncommon in these conditions, suggesting alternative Treg effector functions are sufficient to maintain toler­ ance to self-antigen. Section 3: Inflammatory bowel disease–associated mucosal adaptive responses Loss of tolerance to self and microbial antigens (the ‘holobiont self’) is an early checkpoint in IBD patho­ genesis and can exist in a predisease state. Antimicrobial antibodies and autoantibodies are detected many years before clinical diagnosis of IBD [48–50], and among healthy first-degree relatives antimicrobial antibodies are associated with future disease development [48]. Pa­ tients with established IBD have extensive loss of tol­ erance, as demonstrated by recent multiplexed immunoglobin detection arrays, which identify hundreds of disease-associated antimicrobial and anti-self anti­ bodies [51–53]. The characteristic serological responses of IBD (Supplementary Table 1), many of which were identified several decades ago, are high-titre and prevalent examples of a much larger group of IBD-associated mucosal adaptive responses. This group encompasses T and B cell responses and includes host-protective, by­ stander, and pathogenic examples. They have potential utility as biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Pathogenic T cell responses In health, a large, clonally diverse population of com­ mensal-specific CD4+ T cells respond to highly ex­ pressed conserved microbial epitopes with predominantly barrier-supporting and immunoregulatory effector functions [18,54]. In IBD, there is complex dysregulation of the CD4+ T cell response [18], with increased Th1 and pro-inflammatory Th17 subtypes and decreased Tregs. The TCR repertoire is clonally ex­ panded and has reduced diversity [55], indicating pa­ thogenic activity against a restricted pool of antigens. Clonal expansions are predominantly private and di­ rected against unidentified antigens [19]. However, several antigen-specific pathogenic CD4+ T cell re­ sponses have been identified, particularly against the targets of antimicrobial antibodies (Figure 2). Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA) recognise structurally related yeast oligo-mannans on the cell wall of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Candida albicans, and other yeasts [56]. Pathogenic antibody formation Abnormal B cell activation in IBD results in clonal ex­ pansion, reduced diversity, and a marked increase in IgG+ plasmablasts and plasma cells [63,67]. Anti-com­ mensal IgG antibodies are increased and can have a di­ rect pathogenic effect [52,53,67]. Commensal-IgG complexes engage FcyRIIA on innate immune cells, provoking IL1B release and a Th17 response [68]. An IgG-mediated macrophage activation signature is de­ tectable in ulcerative colitis (UC) anti-TNF non­ responders [67], and polymorphisms that reduce the affinity of FcγRIIA for IgG protect against UC [68]. Si­ milarly, a glycosylated ASCA IgG isoform, which is specific for CD and present prediagnosis, triggers a pro- inflammatory response via FcyRIIA binding and in­ creases colitis severity in mice [69]. IBD-associated autoantibodies can cause or exacerbate intestinal inflammation when they impair host-protec­ tive responses or neutralise tolerogenic signalling path­ ways (Figure 2). In Crohn’s disease (CD), several autoantibodies are associated with complex ileal disease (Supplementary Table 1) and interfere with barrier or innate antimicrobial function. Anti-GM-CSF antibodies neutralise GM-CSF, destabilising the homeostatic interaction between IECs and innate im­ mune cells. CD patients with anti-GM-CSF antibodies have altered monocyte retinoic acid production, leading to dysregulated, pro-inflammatory ILC1s [50]. This is ac­ companied by increased intestinal permeability [70] and reduced neutrophil phagocytic capacity [71]. Anti- GM-CSF antibodies are also associated with pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP). Conclusion Insights from a holobiont perspective From a holobiont perspective, symbiotic microbial communities and self-antigen are both components of the ‘holobiont self’ and must be tolerated to maintain intestinal mucosal homeostasis. To achieve this, the adaptive immune system employs different im­ munoregulatory effector functions. Contact-dependent suppression by Tregs has a prominent role in preventing responses to self-antigen, while the Treg-monocyte/ macrophage IL10 signalling axis is critical in regulation of antimicrobial responses. There is some overlap but limited redundancy between these mechanisms. Functional defects in these systems lead to loss of tol­ erance to the ‘holobiont self’. This is an important early event in pathogenesis of IBD, often preceding diagnosis. The resulting IBD-associated mucosal adaptive re­ sponses include inappropriate T and B cell responses to microbial, self, and environmental antigens. Therapeutic implications With increasing use of TCR-clonotyping and multi­ plexed immunoglobulin detection arrays, the full extent of IBD-associated mucosal adaptive-immune responses is being revealed. These studies identify a combination of shared and patient-specific antimicrobial and anti-self- adaptive responses. Known IBD-associated mucosal adaptive responses have been assessed as biomarkers for the diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic stratification of IBD. The sensitivity and specificity of most is insufficient for routine clinical use (Supplementary Table 1), though interesting disease associations have been noted. Several serological mar­ kers for IBD are associated with increased prevalence of extraintestinal manifestations, disease location, and dis­ ease severity (Supplementary Table 1). There is in­ sufficient evidence to comprehensively assess other interesting associations, such as response to treatment, or sex-associated differences in antimicrobial immunity and autoimmunity in IBD. Further profiling of IBD-associated adaptive responses may identify novel clinically useful biomarkers, this may include responses to the intestinal virome, which is al­ tered in IBD and a target of serological responses in UC [52,84]. Alternatively, an increased understanding of patient-specific and shared adaptive immune responses may lead to the development of complex biomarkers, based on patterns of reactivity to groups of microbial, viral, and self-antigens. The recent discovery of anti- integrin αvβ6, which has good diagnostic accuracy for UC, and glycosylation-specific IgGs, which have promise as a diagnostic biomarker for CD [69], demonstrates the potential for novel biomarker discovery in IBD. Beyond their utility as biomarkers, identifying IBD-as­ sociated mucosal adaptive responses could facilitate de­ velopment of highly targeted therapeutics. This could involve the identification and treatment of patients with high-titre of deleterious autoantibodies (e.g. neutralising anti-IL-10 antibodies) with B cell and plasma cell–tar­ geted therapies. Anti-CD20 (rituximab) is not effective in undifferentiated IBD patients [85] but could be in this selected cohort. Alternatively, anti-CD19 anti­ bodies, which provide broader B cell depletion, or anti- CD38 antibodies, which target plasma cells, may provide greater benefit. In addition, patients with autoantibody- mediated disturbance of homeostatic or host-defence mechanisms could receive targeted treatments to restore disrupted pathways. For example, unglycosylated GM- CSF as a potential therapeutic strategy for patients with anti-GM-CSF neutralising antibodies [50]. Targeting antigen-specific T cell responses also holds promise. For example, patients with a significant anti­ flagellar CD4+ T cell response could have selective depletion of antiflagellar effector T cells [86] or receive antiflagellar chimeric-antigen-receptor regulatory T cells [87] to reduce pro-inflammatory responses. In conclusion, inappropriate adaptive immune responses to the holobiont make an important contribution to the pathogenesis of IBD. They are the primary driver of disease in some cases and likely a disease amplifier in a much larger group of patients. Results: Real-time qPCR revealed significant differences (p-value <0.05) in the abundance of several bacterial groups between IBD patients and healthy controls. Firmicutes, Fusobacterium spp., and B. fragilis were signifi­ cantly more abundant (p-value <0.05) in IBD patients compared to controls. Conversely, Lactobacillus spp. and F. prausnitzii were both significantly less abundant (p-value <0.05) in IBD patients. While some bacterial groups exhibited trends toward higher abundance in either CD or UC patients, these differences were not statistically significant (p-value >0.111). The correlation matrix analysis revealed specific co-occurrence patterns: Bacteroides showed a strong negative correlation with Prevotella, more abundant in healthy controls, suggesting a shift in dominance in IBD patients. Lactobacillus spp. and F. prausnitzii exhibited a positive correlation in healthy in­ dividuals, indicating their potential cooperative role in maintaining gut homeostasis. Conclusion: This study identified significant alterations in gut microbiota composition in adult IBD patients compared to healthy controls, with notable differences in the abundance of specific bacterial groups. These findings suggest that gut microbiota dysbiosis may play a critical role in IBD pathogenesis. The identification of specific bacterial imbalances provides a foundation for developing microbiota-based therapies, such as pro­ biotics, prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation, as potential interventions for restoring microbial bal­ ance and mitigating disease progression. Further research is needed to translate these insights into targeted therapeutic strategies and to explore their effectiveness in clinical settings. 1. Introduction The gut microbiota plays a pivotal role in maintaining gastrointes­ tinal health through its contributions to metabolism, immune system regulation, and protection against pathogens [1,2]. Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), which includes Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract that has been increasingly linked to disturbances in the gut microbiota, commonly referred to as dysbiosis [1]. Identifying consistent patterns of microbial alterations associated with IBD could help bridge gaps in knowledge and enable the development of microbiota-focused therapies [6,7]. In this study, we utilized real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) to investigate the differences in gut microbiota composition between adult IBD patients and healthy controls. By focusing on bacterial groups known to influence gut health, this research aims to provide new in­ sights into the role of gut microbial dysbiosis in IBD pathogenesis and its potential implications for therapeutic intervention. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study subjects samples collection This case-control study was conducted at the Golestan University of Medical Sciences in Gorgan, Iran, and included 60 adult participants (30 IBD patients and 30 healthy individuals). Among the IBD patients, 13 had CD and 17 had UC, who visited the Gastroenterology Department of Sayyad Shirazi Hospital between 2022 and 2023. The participants’ ages ranged from 18 to 74 years (mean age, 45 ± 35 years), and their body mass indices (BMI) ranged from 18 to 36 kg/m2. IBD diagnosis followed the guidelines of the European Crohn’s and Colitis Organization. Patients with autoimmune, inflammatory, or in­ fectious diseases, malignancy, or a history of treatment affecting gut microbiota within three months of study participation were excluded. Patients completed a questionnaire providing demographic, clinical, and additional information like birthplace, residence, marital status, occupation, education, ethnicity, personal habits, extraintestinal symp­ toms, medication intake, and IBD family history. Informed consent was obtained before specimen and data collection, and 18 matched individuals were included as controls. Discussion The results of this study contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting the pivotal role of gut microbiota dysbiosis in the patho­ genesis of IBD, which includes both CD and UC. Through real-time qPCR analysis, we have identified significant alterations in the abundance of various bacterial groups in adult IBD patients when compared to healthy controls. In comparison with other studies, our findings both corroborate and expand upon the existing understanding of gut microbiota dysbiosis in IBD patients. Several studies have reported a decreased abundance of beneficial bacteria, such as Lactobacillus spp. and F. prausnitzii, in IBD patients, which is consistent with our observations. For instance, a study by Machiels et al. (2017) [11] found a lower abundance of Lactobacillus spp. in IBD patients, while F. prausnitzii depletion has been reported in various studies, including those by Willing et al. (2009) [12] and Sokol et al. (2009)([13]). These findings underscore the potential importance of these bacterial groups in maintaining intestinal homeostasis and mitigating inflammation. We also observed an increased abundance of Firmicutes, Fusobacte­ rium spp., and B. fragilis in IBD patients, which is in line with previous research. Manichanh et al. (2006) [14] reported an increase in Firmi­ cutes in IBD patients, while Geirnaert et al. (2014) [15] found a higher abundance of Fusobacterium spp. in IBD patients, particularly in CD patients. B. fragilis, known for its pro-inflammatory properties, has been previously linked to IBD pathogenesis in studies by Rizzetto et al. (2018) [16] and Wang et al. (2021) [17]. These findings collectively suggest that an increased abundance of these bacterial groups may play a role in promoting intestinal inflammation in IBD. This finding emphasizes the complexity of microbial interactions within the gut ecosystem and suggests that the pathogenesis of IBD may involve intricate networks of microbial re­ lationships. Future studies should delve deeper into these interactions and their functional implications to unravel the mechanisms underlying the development and progression of IBD. The lack of significant microbiota differences between Crohn’s dis­ ease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) may be explained by several fac­ tors. Both conditions share overlapping pathophysiological mechanisms, such as immune dysregulation and inflammatory re­ sponses, which can result in similar microbial alterations. Heterogeneity within CD and UC subtypes, such as inflammation location, may obscure differences. Additionally, shared treatments like immunosuppressants or corticosteroids may influence microbiota composition, masking disease-specific variations. Technical limitations, such as the resolution of 16S rDNA qPCR, may also reduce the ability to detect subtle differ­ ences. Functional overlap between the microbial communities in CD and UC may lead to similar disruptions in metabolic or immune interactions, even if taxonomic differences exist. Finally, shared environmental or lifestyle factors, including diet, may homogenize microbiota profiles across IBD patients. This study reveals gut microbiota imbalances in IBD, highlighting opportunities for microbiota-based therapies. Finally, shared environmental or lifestyle factors, including diet, may homogenize microbiota profiles across IBD patients. This study reveals gut microbiota imbalances in IBD, highlighting opportunities for microbiota-based therapies. Restoring microbial bal­ ance through probiotics, dietary changes, or fecal microbiota trans­ plantation could complement existing treatments. Additionally, these findings may aid in developing biomarkers for personalized therapeutic approaches, emphasizing the importance of targeting gut microbiota in managing IBD. This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. The relatively small sample size may limit the generalizability of the results, and the geographic specificity of the cohort may not fully capture global variations in gut microbiota composition. Additionally, the use of 16S rDNA qPCR provides taxo­ nomic insights but lacks resolution for functional analyses of microbial communities. Future studies with larger, more diverse cohorts and multi-omics approaches are needed to validate and expand these findings. To build on these findings, future research should include longitu­ dinal studies to track dynamic changes in gut microbiota over the course of IBD progression and treatment. Mechanistic experiments, such as in vitro and in vivo models, are essential to understand the causal re­ lationships between specific microbial taxa and disease pathogenesis. Additionally, integrating multi-omics approaches, including meta­ genomics and metabolomics, could provide deeper insights into the functional roles of microbial communities. These steps will help trans­ late microbiota-based research into effective therapeutic strategies for IBD. 5. Conclusions Our study provides further evidence on the pivotal role of gut microbiota dysbiosis in IBD pathogenesis, revealing significant alter­ ations in bacterial composition in adult IBD patients compared to healthy controls. These findings underscore the potential importance of gut microbiota in IBD management and support the need for further research on the role of dysbiosis in disease development and progres­ sion. These findings underscore the potential importance of gut microbiota in IBD management and support the need for further research on the role of dysbiosis in disease development and progres­ sion. Introduction Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a chronic recurrent inflammatory disease of the gastrointestinal tract, is composed of Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC).1 These two disorders differ in many respects. CD is characterized by dispersed lesions and transmural inflammation that can occur anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract, with the most frequent symptoms of abdominal pain, diarrhea, fistulae, obstruction, and/or perianal lesions.2 In UC, the lesions are continuous and limited to the mucosal layer of the colon and rectum, which can most commonly lead to bloody diarrhea and rectal bleeding.3,4 The prevalence of IBD is higher in developed countries than developing countries.5 Nevertheless, the prevalence and incidence of IBD are increasing globally, especially in newly industrialized countries.6 Therefore, the disease burden will become ever higher in both developed and developing countries.7 To reduce the disease burden, personalized management, including regular monitoring of disease activity, matching the patients with the proper treatment, and predicting prognosis, is important. Previous studies have referred to a variety of serological and fecal biomarkers, such as serum C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin 6, fecal calprotectin, and lactoferrin, which serve as surrogate markers for the diagnosis and management of IBD.8 However, these available biomarkers could only assist with the activity monitoring and prognosis of IBD to some extent, instead of being considered as a gold standard in the personalized management of IBD.

Metabolomics facilitate the personalized management in inflammatory bowel disease Rirong Chen*, Jieqi Zheng*, Li Li , Chao Li, Kang Chao, Zhirong Zeng, Minhu Chen and Shenghong Zhang Abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic relapsing inflammation and mucosal lesions. Reliable biomarkers for monitoring disease activity, predicting therapeutic response, and disease relapse are needed in the personalized management of IBD. Given the alterations in metabolomic profiles observed in patients with IBD, metabolomics, a new and developing technique for the qualitative and quantitative study of small metabolite molecules, offers another possibility for identifying candidate markers and promising predictive models. With increasing research on metabolomics, it is gradually considered that metabolomics will play a significant role in the management of IBD. In this review, we summarize the role of metabolomics in the assessment of disease activity, including endoscopic activity and histological activity, prediction of therapeutic response, prediction of relapse, and other aspects concerning disease management in IBD. Furthermore, we describe the limitations of metabolomics and highlight some solutions. Therapeutic Advances in Gastroenterology 14 2 journals.sagepub.com/home/tag Given that patients with IBD often exhibit specific metabolomic profiles, metabolomic analysis is a potential tool for identifying diagnostic and therapeutic markers of IBD.9 Metabolomic analysis is a technique with the advantages of high throughput, high sensitivity, and high accuracy for the qualitative and quantitative study of small metabolite molecules in biological samples, including feces, urine, serum, plasma, breath, and biopsy samples. Metabolomic analysis covers a wide range of metabolites with a molecular mass less than 1500 Da, including but not limited to sugars, lipids, amino acids, nucleic acids, organic acids, fatty acids, and some exogenous chemicals.10 Through metabolomics analysis, promising metabolites or models based on metabolites for facilitating accurate diagnosis and personalized management of IBD will be discovered. Although previous studies have summarized the role of metabolomics in the identification of diagnostic markers for IBD and their possible association with pathological mechanisms,9,11–13 few other clinical applications of metabolomics have been reviewed in detail. Therefore, in the present review, we highlight the possible value of metabolomics in evaluating disease activity for IBD, as well as its potential in predicting treatment response and disease relapse. Metabolomics Metabolomics is the qualitative and quantitative study of a suite of small metabolite molecules in biological samples, which symbolizes the metabolic phenotypes of a living system under specific conditions, or in other words, reflects the metabolic response to pathophysiological stimuli or even genetic modification at a certain time point.10 It includes both targeted and untargeted methods. Targeted metabolomics often focuses on specific known metabolic pathways and can be used for the quantification of metabolites. However, untargeted metabolomics tends to analyze a large number of metabolites in a sample without bias and can be used for the identification of unknown metabolites.14,15 In the existing literature, analytes in metabolomics of

These metabolites can be roughly classified as endogenous and exogenous substances. The former includes organic acids such as citrate and succinate, lipids such as sphingolipids and glycerolipids, amino acids such as histidine and cystine, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), glycosylation products, and other endogenous molecules. Exogenous substances including different kinds of xenobiotics have also been mentioned in some studies.11,13 The primary analytical techniques for metabolomics are nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and mass spectrometry (MS) coupled with gas or liquid chromatography.16 NMR spectroscopy distinguishes metabolites by the resonance frequency of nuclei in a magnetic field. Since the frequency and pattern of resonance vary with the chemical environment, each metabolite with a specific molecular structure generates a unique resonance, showing characteristic chemical shifts in the spectra.17 MS, however, ionizes and fragments the compounds into smaller molecules of different mass-to-charge ratios, which can be measured by a detector and then give rise to corresponding mass spectra. Ionization and fragmentation are to a large extent determined by the chemical structures of metabolites, which enables the identification of different compounds. Chromatography used prior to MS analysis physically separates the metabolites so that the detection of individual molecules can be enhanced.18 Both NMR spectroscopy and MS coupled with chromatography are high-throughput techniques and have their own advantages and limitations.19 As compared

Studies have found that changes in the levels of some metabolites in patients with IBD are strongly associated with the severity of disease activity, and models based on metabolomic findings are capable of accurately distinguishing patients with active disease from those in remission. Since researches that focus on metabolomics and clinical disease activity contribute to revealing disease characteristics rather than patient management, in this section, we just review studies aimed at assessing the endoscopic or histological activity of IBD through metabolomics (Table 1). Metabolomic analysis and endoscopic activity Several studies have revealed that a variety of metabolites from different samples are related to endoscopic activity in patients with IBD. Bodelier et al.32 conducted a prospective cohort study of 725 exhaled air samples from 191 patients with CD to explore potential volatile organic compounds (VOCs) to discriminate the active and remission patients. They found that remission patients were characterized with elevated decanal level and reduced concentration of other nine VOCs. Moreover, in breath samples, ethane was mentioned to be positively correlated with the endoscopic score of UC in another study.26 Through metabolomics analysis, several metabolites in urine sample, including ethylmalonate, l-3,4-dihydroxy-phenylalanine, levoglucosan, and propylene glycol, were demonstrated to associate with endoscopic recurrence in CD patients with ileocolonic resection.24 In addition, urine metabolites associated with endoscopic recurrence differed between patients with and without the use of biological agents. These results suggest the impact of biologics therapy in metabolites should be considered in future metabolomic researches. Furthermore, the

Metabolomics for predicting the therapeutic response in IBD Because of the heterogeneity of IBD, there is not one specific therapy that can satisfy all the patients. Thus, the prediction of therapeutic response and matching the right patients with the right treatment are essential in clinical practice. In this section, distinctive metabolomic signatures that might be useful for identifying different responses of patients with IBD after certain therapies are summarized (Table 2). Through metabolomic analysis, several studies have uncovered that metabolite concentration could reflect and even predict the therapeutic response of these biological agents in patients with IBD. Bjerrum et al.48 conducted a retrospective cohort study including 87 patients with IBD and 37 healthy controls to investigate the variation of serum lipid metabolomic profiles after 14-week anti-TNF therapy. They demonstrated that the lipid profiles of patients with IBD were clear discriminated from the healthy controls before anti-TNF therapy. However, only the lipid profiles of patients with remission UC, instead of nonresponse UC or remission CD, became inseparable from the healthy controls after 14-week anti-TNF therapy. These results indicated that patients with UC who responded to anti-TNF treatment had a remarkable serum metabolomic change, which may help for discovering potential prognostic metabolites. In addition to different types of IBD, different biological agents also had distinct impacts in serum metabolites. A sustained increase in serum tryptophan (TRP) levels was observed in patients with IBD who responded to infliximab therapy, while patients nonresponding to infliximab or receiving vedolizumab therapy did not have a significant change in TRP levels.39 Furthermore, metabolomics was capable of exploring promising metabolites or models to predict therapeutic response to biologics in IBD. Metabolomic profiles and therapeutic response of fecal microbiota transplantation Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is an effective method of directly changing the gut microbiota of recipients to normalize the composition, thereby achieving therapeutic benefits.53 As previous studies have shown that FMT is proposed as a therapeutic approach to induce remission in patients with CD and UC.54,55 Several studies have found that changes in metabolomics can reflect disease remission after FMT treatment. One prospective study46 proved that significant alterations in urinary metabolic profiles of patients with CD who experienced clinical improvement or remission were achieved at the pre-second FMT compared with those at pre-first FMT. In addition, Paramsothy et al.44 found that the primary outcome of FMT treatment could be predicted at baseline according to the fecal metabolomic profiles. The increased levels of SCFA biosynthesis and secondary bile acids, as well as the decreased levels of heme and lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, were considered as markers that enabled patients in remission at week 8 to be distinguished from those who did not achieve remission. Similarly, another study of fecal metabolomes of pediatric patients with UC42 confirmed that in responders after FMT, there was a decrease in acetic acid levels and an increase in butyric acid levels. However, stool SCFAs, such as butyrate, were reported to have no correlation with either anaerobically prepared pooled donor FMT effect or disease activity of UC.43 Hence, whether SCFAs can predict the therapeutic response of FMT is still controversial, and additional studies are needed to confirm their roles. Other applications of metabolomic profiling in the management of IBD Some studies have mentioned other possible utilities of metabolomic profiling in IBD management. As noted in a prospective follow-up study of 535 patients with IBD,39 a lower concentration of serum TRP was linked with a higher probability of the need for surgery in patients with IBD. Moreover, Clerc et al.63 found the associations between plasma glycosylation patterns and disease progression, and the need for increased drug potency or surgery, suggesting a reference for therapy and prognosis. In addition, fecal alanine levels were found to be significantly different between pediatric patients with IBD with high perceived stress and low perceived stress.64 Since the stress level was considered as one of the impact factors of future disease activity in patients with IBD,65,66 fecal alanine levels may assist in predicting disease progression and recurrence. Above all, previous studies have demonstrated that age, gender, and environmental factors such as diet, lifestyle, toxins, and cultural trends can influence metabolic phenotypes.70–73 Therefore, both clinical research and applications of metabolomics should take the influence of these confounding factors into account, especially urinary metabolomics, which are thought to be more susceptible to environmental factors than metabolomics of other sample types.70,72 Otherwise, biased results and even erroneous conclusion may be drawn. As noted in a prospective study for relapse prediction of UC, concentrations of plasma histidine and glutamate are affected by age and gender in patients with UC.60 After gender and age adjustment, the association between histidine and the risk of relapse was more obvious, while the opposite was true for glutamate.
