1 | Introduction Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract (GIT) mediated by an altered immune response. IBD includes Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), which are differentiated by the type of inflammation, intestinal location, symptoms and associated complications (Gomollón et al. 2017; Magro et al. 2017). Although the aetiology of the disease is not yet known, current evidence suggests that both UC and CD result from inappropriate immune activation directed against intestinal microorganisms (Rogler 2017). The burden of IBD continues to expand, particularly across Western populations, with European cases reaching approximately 3 million individuals (Kaplan 2015). The immune system can establish a balance between immune responses against pathogens and tolerogenic responses against commensal microbiota (Iebba et al. 2016). In addition to the composition of the intestinal microbiota itself, it is important to highlight that microorganisms generate metabolites, called postbiotics, which have various properties, exert significant immunomodulatory effects. Short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as butyrate, propionate and acetate are products of bacterial action on dietary fiber. These metabolites can modulate histone acetylases during immune responses, thereby affecting gene expression (Tian et al. 2024). Notably, IBD patients demonstrate reduced populations of butyrate‐synthesizing bacteria, such as Roseburia spp (Imhann et al. 2018). Similarly, microbial transformation of tryptophan generates indole‐containing bioactive compounds that engage the aryl hydrocarbon receptor—a transcription factor governing inflammatory processes in immune cells, in the case of IBD, tryptophan metabolism is reduced (Schirmer et al. 2019). Moreover, bacterially‐derived secondary bile acids regulate genetic programs controlling immune cell development, cytokine production, and antimicrobial defence mechanisms (Devlin and Fischbach 2015). This production of secondary bile acids is decreased in patients with IBD (Di Ciaula et al. 2023). Host genetics, environmental exposures, lifestyle patterns, and dietary habits collectively shape gut microbial communities. The transition to a state of dysbiosis can trigger or exacerbate autoimmune and inflammatory responses (Haneishi et al. 2023; Imai et al. 2019; Levy et al. 2017). Amplicon sequencing studies using the 16S ribosomal RNA gene have revealed differences in the mucosal‐associated intestinal microbiota of patients with IBD compared to healthy controls (Gevers et al. 2014), including a depletion of Firmicutes (which have an anti‐inflammatory effect) and Clostridium species, as well as an increase in the abundance of Bacteroidetes and Proteobacteria, such as Bacteroides, Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, which are associated with inflammation (Schirmer et al. 2019; Andoh et al. 2011). Nonbacterial enteric microorganisms, including fungi and viruses, also participate in maintaining gut equilibrium. Although research examining gastrointestinal fungi and viruses in IBD pathogenesis remains limited, dysbiotic patterns within these microbial communities have been implicated in disease development (Iliev and Cadwell 2021). IBD patients exhibit a higher Basidiomycota/Ascomycota ratio, reduced Saccharomyces cerevisiae and increased Candida albicans compared to controls (Sokol et al. 2017). While diverse fungal species inhabit the human gut, only select species show consistent presence across individuals. The enteric virome represents an emerging research frontier given its potential influence on digestive homeostasis (Virgin 2014). However, the high variability observed among individuals complicates the identification of specific relationships IBD‐virome (Finkbeiner et al. 2008; Minot et al. 2011; Ungaro et al. 2019). After assessing the quality of the demultiplexed reads, sequences were denoised using the DADA2 algorithm (Callahan et al. 2016), this process generated a feature table of Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs). During this step, forward reads were trimmed by 6 bp from the 5' end and truncated at 240 bp, while reverse reads were trimmed by 7 bp and truncated at 240 bp. For phylogenetic analysis, sequences were aligned using the MAFT algorithm (Katoh 2002). Taxonomic classification was then assigned to each ASV using a pre‐trained Naive Bayes classifier against the appropriate reference database (SILVA for bacteria and UNITE for fungi). The resulting ASV feature table, taxonomy table and phylogenetic tree were then exported for downstream analysis in R (https://www.r-project.org/). In addition, beta diversity was calculated and plots were generated to help visualize its results. An exploratory analysis was conducted to visualize the microbial composition. Inter‐kingdom associations were investigated by calculating Spearman's rank correlation between the relative abundances of the top 20 bacterial genera and all the detected fungal genera (Akiyama et al. 2024). The decision to use relative abundances despite the compositional nature of microbiome data was due to the fact that the data set used for this study has a small sample size and is highly sparse. were no significant differences, alpha diversity indices revealed distinct microbial patterns. The control group tended to show relatively balanced microbial diversity, with a slight predominance of certain species, although these differences were not statistically significant. In contrast, both active UC and CD groups appeared to have higher microbial diversity with a lower dominance of specific taxa; however, these observations were not supported by significant statistical differences. Notably, the quiescent UC and CD groups tended to exhibit higher diversity and evenness, which may suggest a partial restoration of microbiota composition during remission, though these findings did not reach statistical significance (Figure 1). Beta diversity analysis revealed no significant differences between groups. Bray‐Curtis, Jaccard, and UniFrac (weighted and unweighted) distance metrics were used to assess community composition. Although no statistically significant differences were detected, variability among individuals was evident, suggesting a heterogeneous microbial landscape irrespective of disease status (Supporting Information S1: Figure S1). Having analyzed alpha and beta diversities, we assessed the study of bacterial composition. Distinct bacterial signatures were observed among groups (Figure 2). In control group, Bacteroides, Escherichia‐Shigella and Helicobacter were predominant. However, Helicobacter was associated only with one patient, so its presence in this group is not representative of a characteristic feature of the control cohort. Brachyspira, Erysipelotrichaceae, and Ruminococcus gnavus were detected exclusively in control samples. Active CD patients exhibited a high abundance of Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Prevotella and Faecalebacterium, while in quiescent CD patients, the most abundant genera were Bacteroides, Fusobacterium and Escherichia‐Shigella. Notably Neisseria and Staphylococcus were exclusive to active CD, while Porphyromonas, Plesiomonas and Subdoligranulum were specific to quiescent CD. Cutibacterium was detected in both CD groups, but absent in UC and controls, suggesting its potential association with CD. Results: Periodontitis was significantly associated with increased IBD risk (OR = 4.82, 95% CI: 1.15–20.15, P = 0.031). The IBD group showed reduced Shannon diversity (P = 0.045) without significant β-diversity differences. Severe periodontitis affects more than one billion individuals globally, with its incidence increasing in parallel with population aging, thus constituting a significant public health concern in the realm of oral health [5,6]. Emerging evidence has elucidated a significant intrinsic association between IBD and periodontitis [7]. Both conditions share common pathophysiological mechanisms, notably immune dysregulation, dysbiosis of the microbiota, and sustained inflammation [8]. The aetiology of IBD is multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition, environmental influences, compromised intestinal barrier integrity, and aberrant immune responses to the intestinal microbiome [9,10]. Analogously, periodontitis is characterised by an exagger­ ated inflammatory response to periodontal pathogens, such as Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum, fundamentally reflecting an immune imbalance precipitated by microbial dysregulation [11]. Furthermore, the localised inflammatory process in periodontitis can exert systemic effects through the ‘oral-systemic connection’, leading to the conceptualisation of the ‘oral-gut axis’. This concept underscores the premise that perturbations in the oral microbiome may influence the distal gastrointestinal tract via both direct and indirect mechanisms [12–14]. Epidemiological evidence demonstrates a higher prevalence of periodontitis among individuals with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) compared to the general population, and conversely, IBD is more common in those with periodontitis [8]. Mendelian randomisation analyses have identified Crohn’s disease (CD) as a risk factor for periodontitis, while periodontitis appears to exacerbate ulcerative colitis, thereby supporting the concept of an oral-gut axis [15]. Additionally, smoking—an established risk factor for periodontitis—has been linked to increased genetic susceptibility to CD [16]. Nonetheless, the current body of research is characterised by inconsistencies, which may be attributed to limited sample sizes, confounding variables, and heterogeneity in diagnostic criteria. Consequently, further validation through large-scale, population-based studies remains necessary [14]. Nonetheless, the current body of research is characterised by inconsistencies, which may be attributed to limited sample sizes, confounding variables, and heterogeneity in diagnostic criteria. Consequently, further validation through large-scale, population-based studies remains necessary [14]. Recent advances in microbiome research provide novel insights into the mechanisms underlying the oral-gut axis [17]. The oral cavity constitutes the second largest microbial reservoir in the human body and maintains a dynamic homoeostasis with the host under physiological conditions [18]. In periodontitis, pathogenic symbionts—primarily Gram-negative anaerobic bacteria—undergo excessive proliferation, thereby disturbing this equilibrium [19,20]. Oral microorganisms can reach the gastrointestinal tract via two principal routes: continuous ingestion through saliva and hematogenous dissemination from ulcerated periodontal pockets to distant organs, including the intestine [21]. Animal studies have shown that oral pathogens, such as Porphyromonas gingivalis, can aggravate colitis, compromise intestinal barrier integ­ rity, and alter immune homoeostasis [22]. Research by Atarashi K et al. indicates that the oral cavity may function as a reservoir for potential intestinal pathogens that contribute to the exacerbation of gastro­ intestinal diseases [23]. Furthermore, clinical investigations by Said HS et al. have demonstrated significant alterations in the oral microbiota of IBD patients, including increased abundance of Proteobacteria and decreased counts of Proteobacteria within the salivary microbiome [24]. These findings underscore a pivotal question: Do changes in the oral microbiome serve as an independent risk factor or as a mediating mechanism in the association between periodontitis and IBD? To date, systematic studies integrating clinical phenotypes, comprehensive microbiome profiling, and nationally representative datasets are lacking. To address these knowledge gaps, the present study used data from the 2009–2010 cycle of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), which includes standardised periodontal examina­ tions, self-reported physician-diagnosed inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and oral microbiome profiling based on 16S rRNA sequencing [25–28]. The study had two primary objectives. Second, we aimed to characterise differences in oral microbial diversity, community composition, and IBD-associated bacterial taxa between participants with and without IBD. Materials and methods Study population This study utilised data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), a nationally representative database employing a multistage, stratified sampling design. The survey encom­ passes comprehensive household interviews and physical examinations, aiming to assess the health and nutritional status of the non-institutionalised civilian population in the United States. The NHANES protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the National Centre for Health Statistics (NCHS), and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their inclusion in the survey. Detailed information regarding the survey design, sampling methodology, and laboratory procedures is available on the NHANES official website (http://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes). In this study, we analysed data from the 2009–2010 NHANES cycle because this cycle included standardised periodontal examinations, self-reported physician-diagnosed IBD, demographic and clinical covariates, and oral microbiome sequencing data. The initial sample comprised 10,537 participants, of whom 4,961 had available microbiome data. Among these, a relatively small number (n = 50) were identified as having IBD. Using a 1:1 propensity score matching strategy based on age and sex, we matched the 50 IBD cases to 50 controls, resulting in a final analytic sample of 100 individuals. Independent variable In the NHANES 2009–2012 ‘Oral Health—Periodontal Examination’ protocol, six sites were assessed per tooth, with a maximum of 28 teeth examined per participant. Clinical periodontal measurements comprised two primary indicators: clinical attachment loss (AL) and probing depth (PD). The classifica­ tion of periodontitis in this study adhered to the criteria established by the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention/American Academy of Periodontology (CDC/AAP). Severe periodontitis was defined as the presence of AL ≥ 6 mm at ≥ 2 interproximal sites (not on the same tooth) and PD ≥ 5 mm at ≥ 1 interproximal site. Although sample allocation across plates was not explicitly randomised, standardised protocols were employed, and quality control samples were included on each plate to minimise potential batch effects. Upon arrival, samples were stored at −20 °C until further processing. PCR amplification and sequencing of the 16S V4 region were performed using 515F-806R primers, resulting in 19 independent HiSeq sequencing runs. In cases where a HiSeq run or lane failed (defined as all samples yielding no reads or fewer than 100 reads), affected samples were re-sequenced in subsequent runs. For samples from the same participant sequenced in multiple runs, only the result from the latest (re-sequenced) run was retained. Data processing was conducted using QIIME1, which evaluated the demultiplexed raw sequence files, yielding 10,442 forward and 10,440 reverse fastq files. Due to the limited read length of 125 bp, effective paired-end merging was not feasible; thus, only the forward reads were retained for downstream analysis using the DADA2 pipeline (v. 1.2.1). Each sequencing run was processed independently, and results were subsequently merged. This approach generated amplicon sequence variants (ASVs), which represent unique microbial sequences identified in each sample following quality control [26]. ASVs were catalogued in a feature table documenting the read counts per ASV in each sample. To assess microbial community diversity, α-diversity and β-diversity metrics were calculated using QIIME2. α- diversity, which characterises the diversity within individual samples, was quantified employing four indices: operational taxonomic unit (OTU) richness, Faith’s phylogenetic diversity, the Shannon-Wiener index, and the inverse Simpson index. These indices were computed following rarefaction of all samples to a uniform sequencing depth of 10,000 reads per sample. Subsequent analyses revealed a correlation between OTU richness and Faith’s phylogenetic diversity, as well as between the Shannon-Wiener and inverse Simpson indices. β-diversity was evaluated using Bray–Curtis and Jaccard distance matrices, which characterise abundance-based and presence/ absence-based community dissimilarities, respectively. Principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was used for visualisation. Between-group differences in beta diversity were assessed using PERMANOVA, and within- group dispersion was evaluated using PERMDISP. Discussion In this study, key confounding factors were rigorously controlled using propensity score matching (PSM), in conjunction with multidimensional microbiome analyses, to investigate the epidemiological association between periodontitis and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) as well as the potential oral microbial ecological mechanisms underlying this relationship. After comprehensive adjustment for socioeconomic status, lifestyle variables, and comorbidities, a significant positive association was observed between periodontitis and IBD risk (OR = 4.82, 95% CI: 1.15–20.15, P = 0.031). In contrast, this association did not reach statistical significance in models with no adjustment or adjustment for demographic variables alone. These findings suggest the presence of negative confounding suppression, wherein certain factors inversely associated with both periodontitis and IBD may mask or attenuate the true relationship between the two conditions when not adequately controlled. This interpretation is corroborated by a meta-analysis conducted by Wang Z et al., which similarly demonstrated that confounding factors can bias the observed association between periodontitis and IBD [7]. Additionally, the present study achieved preliminary balance in age and sex through PSM and further incorporated variables such as education and poverty income ratio (PIR) in Model 3, thereby enhancing the robustness of the association. Nevertheless, the possibility of residual confounding cannot be excluded. Notably, the 95% confidence interval for the odds ratio in Model 3 was relatively wide (1.15–20.15), reflecting the limited post-matching sample size and consequent uncertainty in the effect estimate. These findings suggest that oral dysbiosis in IBD is primarily characterised by diminished intra-community diversity rather than a fundamental or large-scale shift in the overall taxonomic composition. This pattern is not unique to our study; similar trends have been observed in other investigations of microbiota associated with chronic diseases. For instance, a case- control study involving a U.S. cohort demonstrated a significant reduction in oral microbial richness among IBD patients compared to healthy controls [35]. Likewise, Molinero N et al. reported a significant decrease in the Shannon diversity index in saliva samples from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC), with β-diversity analysis indicating the formation of two distinct clusters separating UC patients from healthy controls [36]. These results imply that disease states may disrupt the internal dynamic equilibrium of the microbiota, alter interspecies relative abundances, and perturb microbial interaction networks. The proliferation of a limited number of dominant taxa may lead to niche monopolisation and a concomitant reduction in community compositional complexity. Our co-occurrence network analysis corroborated these findings, demonstrating a shift from a previously balanced and diverse microbial network toward a simplified, pathogen-dominated structure under disease conditions, with diminished ecological resilience. Such microecological imbalance is likely to serve as a crucial link mediating the interplay between the two diseases. Regarding the composition of the microbiota, we identified several characteristic microorganisms enriched in either inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) or periodontitis, which facilitates further inference concerning their pathogenic mechanisms. Numerous pathogenic bacteria are recognised as principal contributors to periodontal tissue destruction; notably, several of these have also been detected as colonising the gut, where they may exacerbate IBD [37,38]. Furthermore, our study revealed a significant correlation between the systemic inflammatory status of IBD and the severity of periodontitis. This finding is consistent with the report by Figueredo et al., who observed markedly elevated expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α, in the gingival tissues of patients during active IBD compared to those in remission, with these cytokine levels positively correlating with clinical indices of intestinal disease severity [39]. Multiple additional studies have corroborated these observations [40,41]. Notably, research by Pietropaoli et al. also demon­ strated a significant association between the severity of periodontal disease and IBD severity [42]. These data suggest that systemic inflammation in IBD may disseminate to periodontal tissues, thereby initiating or exacerbating periodontal inflammatory responses. Previous studies have shown that patients with periodontitis exhibit significantly higher serum levels of LPS, IL-1, and IL-6 compared to healthy controls [43], and these inflammatory mediators are known to promote mucosal immune activation and tissue injury in IBD. Based on these findings, a multi-step mechanistic model can be proposed to explain the potential associations among periodontitis, the oral microbiome, and IBD: firstly, periodontitis facilitates extensive proliferation of oral microbes and production of virulence factors [44]; secondly, these oral bacteria and their products may impact the distal gut via two principal pathways—direct translocation through saliva and indirect immune activation—thereby aggravating or precipitating intestinal inflamma­ tion. In this study, we observed reduced oral microbial diversity, an imbalance in the ratio of specific pro- inflammatory and symbiotic taxa, and decreased ecological network stability in IBD patients, which may reflect the

oral bacteria and their products may impact the distal gut via two principal pathways—direct translocation through saliva and indirect immune activation—thereby aggravating or precipitating intestinal inflamma­ tion. In this study, we observed reduced oral microbial diversity, an imbalance in the ratio of specific pro- inflammatory and symbiotic taxa, and decreased ecological network stability in IBD patients, which may reflect the oral manifestations of this pathological cascade. Such alterations in the oral microbial ecosystem may continuously deliver aberrant microbial inputs to the gut or sustain a chronic, low-grade systemic inflammatory state, thereby predisposing to the onset or progression of IBD. It should be emphasised that this proposed model is based on observational data and remains hypothetical; definitive causal relation­ ships and underlying molecular mechanisms require validation through experimental and interventional studies. The strengths of this study are as follows: (1) By integrating epidemiological analyses with high- throughput sequencing technologies, we investigated the association and underlying mechanisms between periodontitis and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) at both the population level and the microbial community level. In contrast to previous studies that focused solely on epidemiological surveys or laboratory research, our approach provides a comprehensive evidentiary chain encompassing both ‘phenomenological associations’ and ‘biological mechanisms’. (2) Our case group includes both major IBD subtypes—Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC)—and is accompanied by detailed clinical data and multiple inflammatory markers. This enables us to explore the influence of IBD subtypes and disease activity on periodontal health, as well as to analyse the role of inflammatory mediators in the comorbidity of these two diseases. (3) We utilised multivariate models to adjust for common confounding factors, thereby minimising confounding bias in the association analyses and enhancing the reliability of our conclusions. (4) In the microbiome analyses, we employed a range of analytical approaches to comprehensively characterise dysbiosis

health, as well as to analyse the role of inflammatory mediators in the comorbidity of these two diseases. (3) We utilised multivariate models to adjust for common confounding factors, thereby minimising confounding bias in the association analyses and enhancing the reliability of our conclusions. (4) In the microbiome analyses, we employed a range of analytical approaches to comprehensively characterise dysbiosis and alterations in microbial interactions, which provides a more systematic and in-depth assessment compared to studies relying on single indicators. Based on the findings and limitations of the present study, future research may be advanced in the following directions: (1) given the relatively small matched sample size and wide confidence intervals, large-scale prospective cohort studies with long-term follow-up are needed to validate whether periodontitis and specific oral microbial profiles can predict IBD risk; (2) randomised controlled trials evaluating the effects of standardised periodontal therapy on IBD activity, relapse, systemic inflammation, and gut microbiota compo­ sition may provide more direct interventional evidence; (3) although α-diversity, β-diversity, taxonomic composition, differential abundance, and co-occurrence network analyses were performed, future studies using metagenomics, metabolomics, metatranscriptomics, and host immunological profiling are needed to better characterise microbial community dynamics and functional pathways along the oral–gut axis; (4) despite propensity score matching and multivariable adjustment, residual confounding cannot be fully excluded, and future studies should collect more detailed data on diet, medication use, antibiotic exposure, oral hygiene behaviours, IBD subtype and activity, and genetic predisposition; and (5) because the correlations between JOURNAL OF ORAL MICROBIOLOGY 17

differential genera and systemic inflammatory markers were generally weak, larger studies integrating repeated inflammatory measurements, paired oral–gut microbiome profiling, and causal inference methods are war­ ranted to clarify the potential mechanistic links among periodontitis, oral dysbiosis, systemic inflammation, and IBD. Conclusion In summary, this NHANES-based study provides population-based evidence that periodontitis is inde­ pendently associated with prevalent IBD after adjustment for multiple potential confounders. In parallel, oral microbiome profiling revealed reduced alpha diversity, alterations in selected bacterial genera, and reorganisation of microbial co-occurrence patterns among participants with IBD. These findings support the relevance of the oral–gut axis and highlight oral microbial dysbiosis as a potential ecological feature associated with IBD. Given the cross-sectional design and limited matched sample size, the findings should be interpreted as association-based and hypothesis-generating. Future large-scale prospective studies integrating detailed clinical phenotyping, deeper microbiome profiling, and host inflammatory measure­ ments are warranted to validate these observations and clarify the biological role of oral microbial alterations in IBD. We then used functional principal component analysis to derive the time-varying trajectory for each marker, which then was used in a multivariate model to predict disease status. Predictive performances at different prediagnosis timepoints were evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUROCs). RESULTS: We identiﬁed a panel of 51 protein biomarkers that were predictive of Crohn’s disease within 5 years with an AUROC of 0.76 and a diagnosis within 1 year with an AUROC of 0.87. Based on the proteins included in the panel, imminent development of CD was associated with changes in the complement cascade, lysosomes, innate immune response, and glycosaminoglycan metabolism. Serum antibodies and proteins identiﬁed patients who received a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis within 5 years with an AUROC of only 0.56 and within 1 year with an AUROC of 0.72. CONCLUSIONS: We identiﬁed a panel of serum antibodies and proteins that were predictive of patients who will receive a diagnosis of Crohn’s disease within 5 years with high accuracy. Methods Study Design and Patients This was a case-control study, nested within a cohort study, described elsewhere (Figure 1).6 Brieﬂy, cases with an incident diagnosis of CD and UC were identiﬁed between 1998 and 2013 within the Defense Medical Surveillance System (DMSS) and linked to the DoDSR.7 Incident cases of IBD had 2 or more medical encounters with an International Classiﬁcation of Diseases, Ninth Revision (ICD-9) code for CD (555.0, 555.1, and 555.9 [including all subgroup codes]) or UC (556 [including all subgroup codes]) and available serum from the time of IBD diagnosis (±1 year) and from the preceding sampling points. Date of IBD diagnosis was the ﬁrst time an IBD ICD-9 code was registered.6 Overall, 1000 CD cases, 1000 UC cases, and 500 healthy control (HC) cases were selected from the DMSS database following a prespeciﬁed algorithm published elsewhere6 and described in the supplementary material. For this nested cohort study, 200 CD, 200 UC, and 200 HC cases were further selected as follows. Because samples were irregularly distributed over time (because of serum availability in the DoDSR) and timepoints not well aligned, a 2-step strategy for data analysis was adopted. First, using markers’ abundance available for each patient before diagnosis, functional principal component analysis was performed to estimate the trajectory through time of different markers for each patient.9–11 Functional principal component analysis models the abundance of each marker as a function of time via a stochastic process, to capture the change along time of each marker. Principal component models were estimated based on samples in the training data, and for each sample in the training and testing data, the abundance of each marker was predicted over time (Supplementary Figure 3). Then, predicted markers’ abundances at a particular time before diagnosis was used in a regression model to predict the disease of interest (ie, CD or UC) (see supplementary material). Discussion The DMSS, when integrated with the DoD-SR, is a large, unique resource that provided us the opportunity to examine the serologic progression of IBD before its clinical onset. The main observation is that it is possible to predict CD up to 5 years before diagnosis by using a panel of antibodies and protein biomarkers. Furthermore, pathway analysis based on proteomics showed that several biomarkers mapped to pathways were associated with the complement cascade, innate immunity, glycosaminoglycan metabolism, and lysosome, suggesting that these biological processes are activated many years before diagnosis. The concept of a preclinical phase of disease in IBD was initially suggested by data from a small military cohort, where patients displayed positive ASCA or ANCA antibodies in a signiﬁcantly higher proportion than control individuals years before diagnosis.19 This was followed by 2 small studies where it was shown that the combination of multiple markers (ASCA-IgA and IgG, anti-Cbir1, anti-OmpC, and pANCA) had better predictive accuracy than each marker alone20 and that the abundance of inﬂammatory biomarkers (high-sensitivity CRP and IL6) was signiﬁcantly higher in patients before IBD diagnosis than in control individuals.21 Moreover, in our previous study, using a different set of samples from the PREDICTS cohort and with no control group, we also showed that those patients with CD who develop complications at diagnosis present higher titer values and numbers of antimicrobial markers in their serum years before diagnosis.5 These studies provided preliminary evidence, that, similar to other immune-mediated inﬂammatory diseases, IBD also may have a preclinical phase that might be reliably detected by disease-speciﬁc biomarkers. However, these prior studies were hampered by a small number of patients and samples, lack of longitudinal prediagnostic samples, and limited number of biomarkers investigated. to other immune-mediated inﬂammatory diseases, IBD also may have a preclinical phase that might be reliably detected by disease-speciﬁc biomarkers. However, these prior studies were hampered by a small number of patients and samples, lack of longitudinal prediagnostic samples, and limited number of biomarkers investigated. Additionally, predictive accuracy was not evaluated on any validation set, and therefore, these studies were not able to assess whether the selected model incurred overﬁtting. Here, we have successfully overcome these prior limitations. Leveraging our access to multiple prediagnosis samples up to 5 years before clinical diagnosis in a wellcharacterized cohort followed over time and our ability to test a large array of markers and handle high-dimensional data, we were able to rigorously study and internally validate the temporal association of biomarkers with the disease of interest. In addition, the functional role in disease pathogenesis of the selected proteomic markers was assessed through comprehensive pathway analysis. Using the SomaLogic platform, we have, for the ﬁrst time to our knowledge, identiﬁed a panel of highly sensitive candidate protein biomarkers for the prediction of CD, with a6% accuracy at 5 years before diagnosis and 88% accuracy at 1 year before diagnosis. Overall, 51 protein biomarkers were found predictive of CD, with 57% overlapping at least 2 different timepoints. The most consistent proteomic markers preceding disease diagnosis were markers of inﬂammation (CRP, serum amyloid P, trypsin 2), markers involved in cytokine signaling, innate immunity, and response to bacteria (complement factors, tumor necrosis factor receptor subunits, lipopolysaccharide binding protein, proteinase-3, and several interleukins). This preclinical phase is of unknown duration but conceivably could start many years before diagnosis. It is know that early intervention in CD is associated with better outcomes25; therefore, it is conceivable that interventions introduced during an even earlier preclinical phase of disease could more easily abrogate or modulate the dysregulated immune responses. However, it remains unclear which interventions could offer the potential to ameliorate or reverse the immunologic changes in this phase. Once disease is established, it becomes difﬁcult to distinguish between the pathways that may be responsible for disease initiation from those resulting from the dysregulated cycle of inﬂammation. We hypothesized that performing pathway analysis on the proteomic biomarkers with the highest predictive performance for IBD with cross checking against multiple well-annotated databases might identify candidate pathways that have biologic plausibility in preclinical IBD pathogenesis. Indeed, by using the SOMAscan proteomic assay spanning a broad array of biological processes, we were able to identify several dysregulated pathways in preclinical CD that could be informative for preventive and therapeutic interventions. The lysosome pathway, deeply interrelated with autophagy, one of the main defective processes in IBD, was signiﬁcantly enriched in patients with CD in comparison with control individuals, especially at 4 years before diagnosis.26 Pathways involved in glycosaminoglycan metabolism were enriched in patients with pre-CD as compared to HC individuals, which is interesting given the accumulating evidence linking defects in glycosylation to inﬂammation and IBD. We can hypothesize that acquiring this type of mechanistic information in preclinical disease can potentially uncover key pathogenic events and lead to the development of new therapeutic targets. Speciﬁcally, pANCA, the most speciﬁc marker for UC, had a suboptimal performance, especially in the most distant years; this ﬁts with the clinical observation that usually UC has a more abrupt clinical presentation and may imply a shorter preclinical period; alternatively, different biological pathways underlying disease initiation and not captured in our biomarker platform may exist. Being a mucosal disease, it is also plausible that mucosal or stool biomarkers could be more appropriate for the prediction or earlier detection of disease. Our work has several strengths and limitations. We used prediagnostic samples from a well-characterized cohort, allowing for a particularly rigorous analysis and internal validation within our cohort. Having access to multiple prediagnosis timepoints allowed us to model the timevarying trajectories by using a stochastic process able to capture the change along time of each marker. Furthermore, we measured a wide selection of markers and used a novel proteomic platform, which, for the ﬁrst time to our knowledge, allowed us to identify putative biological pathways enriched in preclinical disease. Our study is not without some limitations, particularly reliance on serum only, imperfect demographic matching, and generalizability, given that it was restricted to young, predominantly male, active duty military personnel. Some covariates, including tobacco use and family history, known to modulate disease risk were not available. Furthermore, it is possible that in some patients with CD, disease was already established but not recognized because of the delayed diagnosis or absence of symptoms; however, the prediction of markers 5 years before diagnosis likely extends well beyond the reported diagnostic

Finally, the biomarkers identiﬁed and the pathway analysis may have been limited by the background chosen from SomaLogic, enriched in markers involved in inﬂammation and immunity. Because we excluded other immune-mediated diseases from the HC population, we cannot assess the predictive accuracy of the set of biomarkers identiﬁed in these conditions; however, the fact that autophagy, a CD-speciﬁc process, was found to up-regulated suggests that our biomarkers maybe disease speciﬁc. The addition of antimicrobial markers (not usually present in other immunemediated conditions) to the predictive tool, even if its overall predictive accuracy was lower than SomaLogic alone, further improves the marker’s speciﬁcity. In summary, our data suggest CD may be predicted years before diagnosis, but we could not identify predictors for UC. We believe our work represents an important foundation for future work in the preclinical phase of disease. Our 102 Torres et al Gastroenterology Vol. 159, No. 1 CLINICAL AT

results should be validated in independent populations, and the performance of our predictive tool should be improved with genetic, microbiome, and relevant clinical data (eg, smoking, family history) obtained from ongoing longitudinal cohorts. Such multidimensional predictive tools could be used in prospective studies or disease prevention trials to select a priori populations at high risk for developing IBD. IBD prediction and prevention may be a possibility in the future, and it is clear that further research in this ﬁeld is warranted. In the future, early identiﬁcation of individuals at high risk for disease development could allow for close monitoring and for the development of interventions to delay, attenuate, or even halt disease initiation. C rohn’s disease (CD) is one of the inﬂammatory bowel diseases (IBDs) characterized by chronic, relapsing inﬂammation of the intestine. The cause of CD is unknown, but the current hypothesis is that microbial or environmental factors induce gut inﬂammation in genetically susceptible individuals, leading to chronic intestinal inﬂammation and damage.1,2 Case-control studies of patients with established CD have cataloged alterations in the gut microbiome composition3–7; however, these studies fail to distinguish whether the altered gut microbiome composition is associated with initiation of CD or is the result of inﬂammation or drug treatment.3 To address these issues, the Crohn’s and Colitis Canada Genetic Environmental Microbial (GEM) project, a prospective cohort study of healthy ﬁrst-degree relatives (FDRs) of individuals with CD, was designed to identify the parameters associated with the development of CD. Among these parameters, we were interested in proﬁling the gut microbiome composition that precedes the onset of CD and to what extent this composition predicts the risk of developing CD. Speciﬁcally, we applied a machine learning approach to the analysis of the gut microbiome composition in a large cohort of healthy FDRs of patients with CD (N ¼ 3483) to deﬁne a microbial signature that is associated with the risk of developing CD. Construction of the Microbiome Risk Score The gut microbiota is increasingly recognized as an ecologic niche comprising many different taxa that act as a community.11,12 In this context, changes in the abundance of a given bacterial taxon can impact the capacity of other taxa to thrive in a given environment. To address this complexity in the microbiome, we applied a random survival forests (RSF) methodology to assess the relationship between the baseline gut microbiota community and the future risk of developing CD.13 Using this approach, we developed a risk score that combines the effects of relative abundances of bacterial genera, as deﬁned by stool 16S rRNA sequencing in a nonlinear, nonparametric manner, to quantify an individual’s risk of developing CD (see Supplementary Methods). The RSF model allows for combining the high-dimensional microbiome composition data and generating a score that quantiﬁes the risk of developing CD.13 The RSF model can efﬁciently handle the relatively small number of events compared with the large number of nonevents using resampling techniques.13,14 Finally, the RSF model detects and incorporates high-order interactions of the variables, which contribute to the risk score.13,14 Besides the relative abundances of bacterial taxa, the RSF model included the covariates age, sex, Shannon alpha diversity, and the number of sequencing reads (see Supplementary Methods). To develop the risk score model and to ensure its predictive ability, we ﬁrst randomly assigned two-thirds of the original cohort into a discovery cohort and one-third into an independent validation cohort. More precisely, the subjects in the validation cohort were never used in the model construction. The discovery cohort was used to develop the risk score

Discussion Until now, most studies suggesting involvement of the microbiome in CD have been cross-sectional case-control studies of patients with established CD. However, CD activity of inﬂammation and related treatment in those with established disease may introduce confounding effects on the microbial composition. The use of prospective preclinical cohort studies minimizes such confounders and is a more powerful approach to characterizing the contribution of the microbiome to CD onset.20,21 However, due to the rare incidence rate of CD, prospective studies require signiﬁcant time and resources to observe a meaningful number of incident cases. To address these issues, the CCC GEM project, a prospective cohort study of healthy FDRs of individuals with CD, was designed to identify the parameters associated with the development of CD. Using data collected from the GEM cohort, we developed an MRS model from a subset of the original cohort capable of classifying individuals that later go on to develop CD. We hypothesized that differences in the baseline gut microbiota composition between healthy individuals who later develop CD compared with those who remain healthy provide insight in the microbial determinants of CD pathogenesis. However, when we included the fecal calprotectin indicator in the model, the MRS yielded an HR of 1.42 per SD (95% CI, 1.02–1.98 per SD; P ¼ .041) (Supplementary Table 16 and Supplementary Figure 15). The slight decrease in the HR suggests that the MRS is not greatly confounded by the absence or presence of subclinical gut inﬂammation, as reﬂected by elevated fecal calprotectin. Notably, when considering adjusting for continuous fecal calprotectin levels, we found evidence of a nonlinear effect of fecal calprotectin on CD risk (Supplementary Figure 20). Adjusting for both nonlinear and linear components of continuous fecal calprotectin should be further explored in future studies that are appropriately powered to account for this non-linear effect. Another potential limitation of our study is that our ﬁndings are representative of the healthy at-risk FDR population and thus may not pertain to the general population. Moreover, although the MRS was statistically associated with future onset of CD, the predictive performance of the MRS remains relatively modest, indicating that the microbiome in combination with other factors, such as genetic risk and dietary pattern, may improve the risk stratiﬁcation of CD onset among healthy FDRs. Finally, we only have access to a single time point, which means that dynamic changes in individuals that could lead to disease may not be captured. disease onset. Experimental studies will be needed to assess whether the associations presented in this study represent a cause or effect of CD pathogenesis. Nevertheless, we believe that our study sets a framework for future prospective cohort studies to examine the relationship between microbial composition and the risk of developing chronic immune-mediated diseases such as CD. Conclusion This study is the ﬁrst to demonstrate that gut microbiome composition is associated with future onset of CD, which suggests that the gut microbiome is a potential contributor in the pathogenesis of CD. We further demonstrated that microbiome composition can deﬁne an individual’s risk to develop CD according to our prediction model. The involvement of the microbiome in disease onset was validated in an independent cohort and remained associated when adjusted for inﬂammation as measured by fecal calprotectin, and the derived MRS predictability persisted even when the MRS was measured >5 years before disease onset. Integration of the MRS with other biomarkers for improved risk stratiﬁcation remains to be explored in future studies. Understanding the biomarkers associated with the risk of CD and the biology of these biomarkers as they relate to pathogenesis will also be necessary to develop novel strategies for disease prevention in high-risk populations and for improvement in treatment in patients with established disease. RESEARCH LETTERS Development and Validation of an Integrative Risk Score for Future Risk of Crohn’s Disease in Healthy First-Degree Relatives: A Multicenter Prospective Cohort Study D espite advances in medical therapy, approximately one-half of patients with Crohn’s disease (CD) develop complications ultimately requiring surgery. Currently, no treatment offers a chance of cure.1,2 The increasing incidence and prevalence of CD globally pose a substantial burden at the population and individual levels. Thus, a better understanding of the early triggers of CD is desperately needed to enhance early detection, improve medical therapy, and offer a possibility of interventions that prevent development of CD. Previous studies have reported candidate predisease biomarkers associated with future development of CD, supporting the concept of a preclinical phase.3–6 However, these studies lack integration of individual predisease signatures and the multidimensional mechanisms of disease pathogenesis. To date, no risk-stratiﬁcation model has combined multiple predictive biomarkers to predict future risk of developing CD in healthy at-risk individuals. In this study, we leveraged a large prospective multicenter cohort of healthy ﬁrst-degree relatives (FDRs) of people with CD—the Crohn’s and Colitis Canada-Genetic, Environmental, Microbial (GEM) study. Using available demographic characteristics, physiologic biomarkers, and fecal microbiome data, we developed an integrative multidimensional risk model—the GEM integrative risk score (IRS)—that predicts an FDR’s future risk of developing CD. We subsequently validated the performance of GEM-IRS in 2 testing cohorts. We included participants with a minimum 3 months of follow-up duration as of February 28, 2021; participants recruited from countries with sufﬁcient median follow-up duration of at least 5 years (ie, Canada, United States, and Israel); and participants with a complete set of blood, urine, and stool samples at recruitment. To gain further insight into the contribution of individual biomarkers, we estimated feature importance; FCP and LMR were the strongest contributors to the model, followed by microbial composition and functional pathways. Network analysis revealed complex interactions between the microbial composition and functions with FCP and LMR. In addition, heatmap and dendrogram analyses identiﬁed clusters of microbial composition and functions that were associated with increased or decreased risk of CD (Figure 1 and Supplementary Material). To date, this is the ﬁrst description of an integrative risk model that combines physiological biomarkers of gut inﬂammation and gut barrier function with fecal microbial composition and functional pathways to assess the future risk of CD among healthy FDRs. The GEM-IRS showed competitive performance in the testing cohorts from 2 different geographic locations (North America and Israel) and provided the relative risk and cumulative incidence based on individual’s risk scores. In the subset of FDRs with baseline FCP < 50 mg/g or LMR < 0.025, using stringent cutoffs,4,9 we speculated that other factors, for example, gut microbiome composition and functions, could be early events contributing to the risk of developing CD. In our model, the genera Holdemania, Gemella, and Ruminococcus torques group were associated with an increased risk of CD, whereas Anaerosacchariphilus species, Angelakisella, and Lachnospira were associated with a decreased risk. Interestingly, fucose degradation-related microbial pathways were identiﬁed as strongly associated with an increased risk of CD. Indeed, previous gene-wide association studies linked an increased risk of CD with FUT2-null alleles, supporting the role of fucosylation in protection from CD.10 We believe the integrative model showed the potential to risk-stratify high-risk individuals among healthy FDRs, which is the ﬁrst step toward designing a primary prevention trial in CD. Further research is warranted to develop a model that is clinically applicable; we also need to validate and calibrate the ﬁndings in external cohorts (given the possible model instability due to a small number of events) and to determine to what extent asymptomatic persons identiﬁed to be at high risk of CD will be willing to undertake interventional therapy. Our results also point toward changes in biomarkers that might direct speciﬁc intervention strategies. Supplementary Materials and Methods Study Design Details of the CCC-GEM study can be found in our earlier article.6 Study Outcome and the Prespeciﬁed Baseline Variables of Interest The primary outcome was the time to diagnosis of CD. The time in the study was deﬁned as the number of years from the date of recruitment to the date of CD diagnosis (for FDRs who developed CD) or the date of last follow-up (for FDRs who remained healthy) based on the follow-up data available as of February 28, 2021. Of note, participants who developed ulcerative colitis were removed from the analysis. The prespeciﬁed baseline variables included in the subsequent risk-stratiﬁcation model analysis were as follows: age, sex, relation to proband (sibling or offspring), CD-multiplex family status (having more than 1 FDR with a diagnosis of CD at recruitment), FCP, LMR, Shannon a-diversity index, total number of 16S ribosomal RNA reads, relative abundance of taxa at the genus level of taxonomy, and relative abundance of imputed microbial functional pathways. Brieﬂy, fecal microbial proﬁling was performed by sequencing the V4 hypervariable region of bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA gene, as reported previously.6 We summarized the Amplicon Sequence Variant table into taxonomic ranks using QIIME2. Samples with <10,000 reads were excluded from the analysis. In addition, genera present in <20% of the samples were excluded for subsequent analysis. The taxonomic table was converted into relative abundance values by dividing the read counts of each taxon by the sum of the read counts of a sample at the genus taxonomic level. Microbial function was imputed using the PICRUSt2 platform.7 We normalized the output abundances of each function by the 16S Amplicon Sequence Variant counts by the picrust2_pipeline.py script. We generated the pathway abundances against the MetaCyc pathway database. Pathways present in <20% of the samples were removed

Statistical Analysis To develop and validate a model, the subjects recruited from North America (Canada and United States) were randomly split 50:50 into the North American training and testing cohorts. The GEM-IRS was trained in the North American training cohort and tested in the North American testing cohort and in the Israeli cohort, both pooled and separately. The data from the 2 testing cohorts were never used in the model training procedure and were kept separate to avoid data leakage. Validation in the Israeli cohort was considered to assess the generalizability of the score across geographical regions. The GEM-IRS was developed using the random survival forest (Scikit-survival 0.16.1 module of the scikit-learn python package [python, version 3.6.1]), a meta-estimator that ﬁts survival trees on subsamples of the dataset and averages the results to control for overﬁtting and integrates baseline parameters into a model that predicts time to event (further detailed in the following section).8 The prespeciﬁed baseline variables (listed above) were included as predictors in the model. Of note, given the high dimensionality of the microbiome data, we excluded microbial genera and microbial functional pathways with a global test P > .2, using Cox proportional hazards regression in the training set. Harrell’s concordance index (C-index) was used to assess the model performance, which measures the probability that the predicted event of 2 randomly selected subjects maintaining the same relative order as their true event times.e1 Feature

Random Survival Forest We used random survival forest (scikit-survival, version 0.15.1 module of scikit-learn python package [python, version 3.6.1]; https://scikit-survival.readthedocs.io/en/ latest/). The random survival forest consists of an ensemble of regression trees that use the nonparametric Nelson-Aalen estimator for estimating the hazard function. For each tree, a subsample consisting of two-thirds of the training set was drawn (with replacement). In addition, for 153.e1 Lee et al Gastroenterology Vol. 168, Iss. 1

each tree, a subset of the variables was randomly selected to be in the set of candidate variables to build the tree. To ﬁnd the optimal hyperparameters, we performed a 5-fold crossvalidation grid search using the training set only, which maximizes the C-index. We used the functions GridSearchCV (scikit-learn, version 1.0.2) and concordance_index_censored from scikitsurvival, version 0.15.1. We searched the hyperparameter space, which comprised number of trees (start ¼ 30, end ¼ 300), max_features (start ¼ 10, end ¼ 20), max_depth (start ¼ 2, end ¼ 4), min_samples_split (start ¼ 2, end ¼ 150), and min_samples_leaf (start ¼ 10, end ¼ 110). The ﬁnal optimum values deﬁned by the cross-validation grid search were the following: number of trees ¼ 40, max_depth ¼ 3, min_samples_split ¼ 10, min_samples_leaf ¼ 90, and max_feature ¼ 15. METHODS: We assessed the Crohn’s and Colitis Canada Genetic Environmental Microbial cohort of healthy FDRs of patients with CD. Genome-wide CD-polygenic risk scores, urinary fractional excretion of lactulose-tomannitol ratio, fecal calprotectin (FCP), and fecal 16S ribosomal RNA microbiome were measured at recruitment. Associations between CD multiplex status and baseline biomarkers were determined using generalized estimating equations models. Cox models were used to assess the risk of future CD onset. RESULTS: There were 4051 participants from simplex families and 334 from CD multiplex families. CD multiplex status was signiﬁcantly associated with higher baseline FCP (P ¼ .026) but not with baseline CD-polygenic risk scores or the lactulose-to-mannitol ratio. CD multiplex status at recruitment was independently associated with an increased risk of developing CD (adjusted hazard ratio, 3.65; 95% conﬁdence interval, 2.18–6.11, P < .001). T he familial nature of inﬂammatory bowel disease (IBD) has long been identiﬁed.1,2 Observational studies have highlighted a positive family history of IBD as a major risk factor for developing the disease,3,4 with this risk being particularly high in ﬁrst-degree relatives (FDRs) of patients with Crohn’s disease (CD). Importantly, there appears to be an additive risk increment of CD onset per additional affected FDR.5 Therefore, individuals within families with multiple affected members, also known as multiplex families, harbor a notably high risk of developing CD. It has been shown that healthy individuals from multiplex families have a higher number of risk alleles in IBDassociated genes compared with healthy individuals from the general population and that the mean number of risk alleles increases with increasing numbers of affected FDRs.5 However, none of the genetic markers could discriminate between individuals from single-case families (so-called simplex families) and those from multiplex families. Thus, genetics is unlikely the sole factor that can explain this increased risk,5 raising the question of what could be driving the increased risk of CD in multiplex families. In the present study, we aimed to identify differences between FDRs from multiplex families vs FDRs from simplex families regarding CD-related genetic risk, gut barrier dysfunction, preclinical gut inﬂammation, and fecal microbiota composition. We further aimed to investigate the risk of future development of CD in participants from multiplex families compared with participants from simplex families, accounting for potential confounders. Materials and Methods Participant Recruitment Participants were recruited as part of the Crohn’s and Colitis Canada Genetic Environmental Microbial (CCC-GEM) project. The CCC-GEM project is an international, multicenter, prospective study recruiting healthy FDRs of patients with CD. The aim of the CCC-GEM project is to identify potential triggers associated with the later development of CD based on baseline characteristics and recruitment samples (serum, urine, and stool). The CCC-GEM recruited asymptomatic FDRs (siblings or offspring) of patients with CD aged between 6 and 35 years. Participants were screened using a standardized questionnaire to exclude individuals with the presence of any gastrointestinal symptoms, known diagnoses, or symptoms suggestive of IBD, celiac disease, or irritable bowel syndrome. Participants were also excluded if they had received antibiotic treatment within 3 months before recruitment. Demographic information and environmental risk data were recorded as previously described.6 After recruitment, participants were contacted by telephone every 6 months to assess for the development of new symptoms or new CD diagnosis. If the participants declared a change in health, including new symptoms or actual diagnosis, then we conﬁrmed with their treating physician the diagnosis based on clinical, endoscopic, histologic, radiographic reports, or a combination of these. All participants or their guardians gave written informed consent. The study was approved by the Mount Sinai Hospital Research Ethics Board (Toronto–Global Project Ofﬁce) and each of the local recruitment centers. LIMITATIONS Biomarkers and multiplex status were assessed only at recruitment, and most of the participants in the Crohn’s disease multiplex families had only 2 affected ﬁrstdegree relatives. Possibly rare allele variants with large effect sizes would not have been captured by the polygenic risk score. CLINICAL RESEARCH RELEVANCE This study conﬁrms previous ﬁndings of populationbased studies of an increased risk of Crohn’s disease onset in ﬁrst-degree relatives from multiplex families. We found that this risk is independent of subclinical gut inﬂammation, gut barrier dysfunction, and genetic burden. We hypothesize that putative environmental factors driving this risk might be enriched in ﬁrst-degree relatives from multiplex families. Discussion To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest prospective cohort study to date examining the effect of being a member of a CD multiplex family on the risk of disease onset and its relationship with several biological factors that potentially may be involved in this observed increased risk. Importantly, we found a 3-fold higher risk of future CD onset associated with the CD multiplex status at recruitment compared with FDRs from simplex families. This risk was independent from genetic burden, gut barrier function, and subclinical intestinal inﬂammation. This stability suggests that the familial aggregation of CD risk is not solely attributable to these known biological markers and genetic predispositions.

Increased intestinal permeability has been described in individuals with CD,30 and in healthy FDRs, it is associated with a higher risk of CD onset as well as with altered gut microbiome composition and functions.14,16 In contrast, we did not ﬁnd a difference in intestinal permeability as measured by LMR between participants from CD multiplex and simplex families. In the absence of an obvious genetic risk factor difference between participants from CD multiplex and simplex families, a deeper exploration of potential environmental differences between multiplex and simplex families is warranted. This study has several strengths. This cohort is the largest to date in which healthy participants from CD multiplex families with a median follow-up of >5 years were prospectively assessed. Moreover, we assessed the association of CD multiplex with several important biomarkers, such as the fecal microbiome, FCP, CD-PRS, and gut barrier function, which are all possibly involved in CD pathogenesis and were previously shown to confer risk of future onset of CD. Several sensitivity analyses showed the robustness of our results. Given that CD usually has a long preclinical phase, it might be argued that the association between CD multiplex status and higher subclinical gut inﬂammation may be due to undiagnosed disease. A recent population-based casecontrol study from Denmark found differences in biochemical and hematologic parameters up to 8 years before diagnosis in patients with CD vs healthy controls.50 Importantly, the associations we report of increased risk of CD onset and higher subclinical gut inﬂammation between participants from CD multiplex and simplex families remained signiﬁcant, even when excluding individuals with <5 years of follow-up. Notwithstanding, this study has some limitations. First, we did not include some factors that might contribute to disease onset, such as environmental factors. Questionnairebased assessments of environmental factors are limited to a set of questions that cannot measure unknown or novel environmental exposures and are prone to recall bias. With novel exposome technologies, future studies may better capture the shared environmental factors contributing to a higher risk of disease in multiplex families. Moreover, household sharing at the time of recruitment could have provided valuable insights into the impact of environmental factors on biomarker differences and future risk of CD. Unfortunately, we did not have information on household sharing between family members at the time of recruitment. Second, each measured biomarker may have intrinsic limitations related to the technique or approach; notably, LMR is an indirect measure of intestinal paracellular permeability and, therefore, may not reﬂect speciﬁc alterations in tight junction proteins. Additionally, newer, more precise assays to assess gut permeability51 were not available at the time of this study and should be considered for use in future studies. Third, the biomarker values and multiplex status were only deﬁned at the time of recruitment, and thus, we could not assess the dynamic changes of these variables over time. Fourth, most of the participants in the CD multiplex families had only 2 affected FDRs vs 1 FDR affected in the simplex group. It is possible that we were not able to capture subtle differences in biomarkers, notably the genetic burden. Fifth, the sample size of the subgroup of CD multiplex with 3 affected FDRs was too small and did not allow appropriate analyses to evaluate whether there was a dose response to the observations we reported. Finally, it is important to note that most of patients with CD do not have an

subtle differences in biomarkers, notably the genetic burden. Fifth, the sample size of the subgroup of CD multiplex with 3 affected FDRs was too small and did not allow appropriate analyses to evaluate whether there was a dose response to the observations we reported. Finally, it is important to note that most of patients with CD do not have an FDR with CD, and therefore, the results described in this study cannot be generalized to all patients with CD. Conclusion In conclusion, we showed that FDRs from multiplex families have a 3-fold higher risk of CD onset, even after adjusting for demographics, subclinical inﬂammation, gut barrier function, and genetic burden compared with individuals from simplex families. Furthermore, we found that high FCP was associated with CD multiplex as well as differentially abundant fecal bacterial taxa. We did not ﬁnd associations between CD multiplex status and gut barrier function or genetic risk. Future studies should comprehensively assess environmental conditions (ie, dietary patterns, metabolomics, and early-life exposomes) to fully unravel the factors driving this increased risk of disease in FDRs from multiplex families potentially involved in the risk of developing the disease in CD multiplex families. risk factors for the development of IBD.3,4 Plausibly, many of these potential risk factors have been shown to cause dysbiosis in the gut microbiome that could predispose to subsequent development of IBD, although the precise cause of IBD is unknown.5,6 IBD historically has been regarded as a disease of developed nations, although in the past 2 decades there has been a shift in the epidemiologic pattern of disease. High-income nations with known high prevalence of disease are seeing a stabilization of incident cases, while a rapid increase of incident IBD has been observed in developing nations.7,8 This suggests that environmental exposures may play a role in mediating the risk of developing IBD. The potential environmental determinants of IBD across various regions is vast, although medications increasingly have been recognized as one broad category of risk factors. Although nonsteroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs), antibiotics, and oral contraceptives have been well studied as risk factors for IBD, when the totality of evidence is assessed critically, these associations remain largely unclear because of the conﬂicting body of literature, heterogeneity between studies, and study design limitations.9,10 Other medications also have been associated with an increased or reduced risk of IBD.11,12 Given the evolving global epidemiology of IBD, further research across more heterogenous populations with robust design is needed to better understand medications as a risk factor for the development of IBD to validate previously demonstrated relationships, as well as to explore previously unreported associations. For baseline medications that were associated signiﬁcantly with the primary outcome, secondary analyses were planned to evaluate short-term (deﬁned as use only at baseline but not at follow-up evaluation) and long-term use (deﬁned as use at baseline and at next follow-up visit). In addition, tests for heterogeneity were conducted for the outcomes of CD and UC individually. Diagnosis was self-reported by participants. Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics for each comparison are provided. Continuous variables are presented as means (and SDs) or medians (and interquartile ranges). Categoric variables are presented as proportions or percentages and compared using the chi-square test. Multivariate logistic regression models were used to evaluate the relationship between medications and the outcome of interest. Odds ratios (ORs) and corresponding 95% CIs for the development of the outcome of interest were calculated and minimally adjusted for age, 2650 Narula et al Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology Vol. 21, No. 10

Discussion In this large prospective cohort study of 133,137 individuals from 24 low-, middle-, and high-income countries, we found multiple associations between medication use and odds of IBD. Use of antibiotics and hormonal therapies including oral contraceptive pills were associated with an increased odds of IBD, as was longer-term use of NSAIDs. For positive associations identiﬁed in our study, similar directional effects were seen for both UC and CD, with no signiﬁcant heterogeneity. We were unable to conﬁrm or identify any other associations that previously have been reported in the literature, including with proton pump inhibitor or statin use.11,12 Our analysis illuminates and expands upon the role that medications may play as an environmental factor associated with risk of IBD. More than 100 genes have been identiﬁed and are implicated in rendering individuals susceptible to IBD, although genetic factors alone are insufﬁcient to account for the increasing prevalence of IBD in developed and developing countries, and the sharp increase of incidence in developing nations.2,16,17 Environmental determinants of IBD increasingly are being recognized, including the role that medications play in altering the intestinal environment, mucosal barrier, and gut microbiome, and the associated increased risk these alterations pose in the development of IBD.17 The global use of medications (both with and without a prescription) has been increasing over the past 2 decades, with a current estimated 1 dose per person per day of medicines in more than half of the world’s population, a 33% increase compared with 2005.18 The largest increase of medication use aligns with regions with some of the largest developmental gains including India, China, Brazil, Indonesia, and Africa, areas that previously had some of the lowest use of medications.18 Given the changing epidemiological pattern of IBD and global medication use, there is a need to better understand medications as potential environmental risk factors for the development of IBD.17 Figure 2. Nonsteroidal Anti-Inﬂammatory Drugs Our analysis showed an association between baseline NSAID use and increased odds of IBD, mainly observed with longer-term use of NSAIDs. Aspirin was recorded separately and also had a similar trend observed for increased odds (aOR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.18–2.29; P ¼ .003). Prolonged NSAID use contributes to the change and destruction of the intestinal barrier that may predispose individuals to developing IBD. This likely is multifactorial including topical effects, reduced prostaglandins, and microbial dysbiosis, which, ultimately, alters gut permeability, motility, and generates oxidative species that together affect and potentially exacerbate inﬂammatory responses.19–22 Previously published literature from prospective cohort studies similarly has shown increased risk of IBD with longer-term NSAID use21 and increased risk of CD in patients with regular aspirin use.23 Moreover, patients with IBD who regularly use NSAIDs have a higher risk of clinically active disease and higher rates of disease relapse.24,25 Antibiotics We also observed that baseline use of antibiotics was associated with increased odds of IBD. The effect of antibiotics on the intestinal environment and relationship with IBD has been investigated extensively. Antibiotic exposure in healthy individuals has been shown to alter the gut microbiota, with increased frequency and duration of antibiotic exposure resulting in persistent dysbiosis.26–28 These changes in gut microbial diversity and loss of protective microbial species secondary to antibiotic exposure has been shown previously to be an environmental risk factor of IBD in a dose-dependent manner; however, robust and consistent data are lacking.29 This inconsistency likely is owing to the heterogeneity of past studies including retrospective and case-control analyses and the inherent limitations of these study designs. Moreover, different classes of antibiotics affect gut microbiome differently. Previous studies have reported differing associations between antibiotic classes and IBD, such as the consistently increased risk with metronidazole compared with other classes.30,31 Although

Oral Contraceptives and Hormonal Medications Hormonal medications used by males or females at baseline and prior/current oral contraceptive use in women at baseline also was associated with increased odds of IBD. Previous literature has shown divergent results with regard to the associations between oral contraceptive pills and IBD. Notably, a strong association between contraceptive pills and CD has been shown in multiple analyses, although the relationship with UC has not been observed consistently.32–34 In postmenopausal women who use hormonal medications, a relationship between increased risk of UC, but not CD, has been reported.32 The precise mechanism underlying the hormonal relationship and risk of IBD and effect on gastrointestinal environment is poorly understood, although it has been proposed that estrogen may affect the humoral immune system and modify the colonic barrier.35,36 Strengths and Limitations Our study had several strengths. This study design overcomes the limitations of many existing studies within this ﬁeld because most were retrospective, case-control designs or used homogenous populations, which limits external validity. However, our study had a few potential limitations. The bulk of the population within PURE were adults aged 35 to 70, and it is unclear if these associations apply to younger individuals, although other cohort studies have shown similar associations among participants of younger ages.21,32,37 There are far more UC diagnoses compared with CD, which likely reﬂects the bimodal nature of a UC diagnosis, with many individuals being diagnosed in their 50s and 60s, in comparison with the lower incidence of CD in older individuals.38 The lower number of CD cases observed in our cohort may have resulted in insufﬁcient power to detect some associations of medications with IBD risk. Because follow-up visits occurred every year, there is a potential for misclassiﬁcation of exposure over time because it is unlikely that all medications assessed in this study were used consistently throughout the follow-up period. In addition, participants self-reported CD and UC diagnoses, and medical records in English were selected randomly to validate diagnoses. Because only a sample of English language medical records underwent veriﬁcation it is possible that some cases of IBD were misclassiﬁed. Although this may introduce bias, misclassiﬁcation would more likely bias associations to the null and not affect results. Furthermore, medication use was collected using a survey that gathered information on whether a participant was taking a medication at least once per week. No data were gathered with regard to dose and duration at study enrollment, or before enrollment. Conclusions As the global burden of IBD increases, it is imperative to identify environmental determinants that may be contributing to this trend. In this study, antibiotics, hormonal medications, oral contraceptives, and prolonged use of NSAIDs were associated with a higher risk of IBD. Additional studies are warranted to further elucidate precise risk proﬁles of medications we identiﬁed, such as duration of therapy, dose, and speciﬁc classes of medications that confer an increased risk of IBD. Nevertheless, this study illuminates the importance of caution in prescribing antibiotics and oral contraceptives, and, if appropriate, discouraging patients from long-term use of NSAIDs to mitigate this established environmental risk of IBD. Supplementary Methods Details Regarding Study Design In short, the ﬁrst and second phases of the PURE study occurred between January 1, 2003, and December 31, 2016. A total of 133,137 participants between ages 20 and 80 years with available data from at least 1 follow-up evaluation were included in this study. Participants from 24 countries were included (Argentina, Bangladesh, Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, Colombia, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Malaysia, Pakistan, Palestine, Philippines, Poland, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Sweden, Tanzania, Turkey, United Arab Emirates, and Zimbabwe). IBD prevalence in 1990 and 2017 for both sexes and all countries included is provided in Supplementary Table 6. The focus of recruitment in PURE was adults between ages 35 and 70 years, although some participants younger than age 35 (n ¼ 547) or older than age 70 years of age (n ¼ 369) were recruited, the majority from China (n ¼ 308) and Malaysia (n ¼ 239). A detailed sampling and recruitment strategy of the PURE study is provided later. Brieﬂy, standardized questionnaires were used to collect participant data at baseline and follow-up visits, which occurred at least every 3 years. Data were collected at the community, household, and individual level. For example, data regarding tobacco use was measured at the community level using tobacco pricing and availability, at the household level using the number of tobacco users per household, and at the individual level using tobacco exposure. New diagnoses of CD and UC were recorded on case report forms during follow-up evaluation. The current analysis considered all outcome events up to April 2, 2021. The PURE study is coordinated by the Population Health Research Institute, McMaster University, and Hamilton Health Sciences in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada.
