chemicals in the ToxCast database that modulate intestinal inflammation, we used a machine learning approach based on a training set that included the 13 chemicals that boosted intestinal inflammation, the 4 chemicals that ameliorated it and 13 representative chemicals that had no effect in our initial zebrafish screen (Fig. 1c–e and Supplementary Table 3). We first eliminated chemicals and bioassays that were poorly correlated with the set of experimentally validated chemicals, or that contained missing values; this resulted in a testing set of 297 chemicals and 233 bioassays (Fig. 1e). We then used a Kruskal–Wallis test to identify the ToxCast bioassays that best discriminated IBD-promoting, IBD-ameliorating and no-effect chemicals in the training set, identifying 16 bioassays that we defined as an IBD bioactivity feature (Fig. 1e, Extended Data Fig. 1m and Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). On the basis of this IBD bioactivity feature, we built a random forest (RF) model to identify in the ToxCast database additional chemicals predicted to worsen intestinal inflammation, using a random walk with restart (RWR) algorithm to rank them (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Table 6). To validate the RF–RWR results, we evaluated the top 20 chemicals predicted to be proinflammatory (Fig. 1f,g); 6 out of 8 chemicals (75%) that were non-lethal at 20 μM boosted TNBS-induced intestinal inflammation in zebrafish. However, genetic factors do not fully explain disease aetiology, and environmental exposures are thought to have a significant role in IBD onset and progression. Considering the multitude of exposures that affect humans in their lifetime, there is an unmet need for methods to evaluate the effects of the environment on IBD and other human disorders. Here we describe an integrated systems approach to identify environmental factors that promote intestinal inflammation and the mechanisms involved. The potential of zebrafish for microbiome research, and the reported effects of genomic31,32 and environmental33 factors on the microbiome, suggest that this approach may also be useful to study the effects of environmental factors on aspects of the microbiome relevant to IBD. Our findings add to recent reports on the contribution of dietary emulsifiers15, oxazoles34 and other environmental factors to the pathogenesis of IBD and its increasing prevalence in industrialized nations. Propyzamide is broadly used for weed control during the production of vegetables, fruits and ornamental plants, and also in golf courses and sport fields. Although propyzamide is metabolized by plants, about 60% of the chemical remains unmetabolized 50 days after its application35. Indeed, propyzamide exposure levels have been estimated by the EPA to be 102 parts per billion (ppb) for surface water and 21 ppb Sanmarco et al. Page 8 Nature. Exposure levels to propyzamide would be expected to be much greater in communities in which higher levels of ground water contamination can occur from propyzamide use, as well as for people working in the agricultural sector who would be more directly exposed on a regular basis. Future studies should determine actual exposure levels in communities with potential high exposure to propyzamide and among agricultural workers, and determine whether other environmental, microbiome and genetic factors synergize with propyzamide during the pathogenesis of IBD. AHR hyperactivation by dioxins has been linked to human pathology43, but these pathogenic effects involve slowly metabolized AHR agonists and not a rapidly metabolized molecule that interferes with AHR signalling like propyzamide. AHR participates in the control of intestinal inflammation and its regulation by the commensal flora32. Propyzamide boosts intestinal inflammation by interfering with the suppression by AHR of pro-inflammatory responses driven by NF-κB–C/EBPβ signalling. Thus, our findings suggest that propyzamide interferes with physiological AHR-dependent anti-inflammatory mechanisms that are activated by endogenous or microbial agonists. On the basis of the systemic distribution of propyzamide detected after oral administration, propyzamide may interfere with the physiological anti-inflammatory effects of endogenous or microbiomeproduced AHR agonists in cells located in the intestine (such as intestinal epithelial cells, T cells and DCs), and also systemically. Graphical Abstract In brief The enteric nervous system relays chronically elevated levels of glucocorticoids to induce transcriptional immaturity in enteric neurons, monocyte recruitment, dysmotility and a general inflammatory state in the gut associated with inflammatory bowel disease INTRODUCTION Psychological stress exerts a profound impact on inflammatory processes throughout the body1–3, suggesting that improving a patient’s mental state might be a powerful yet underutilized strategy for the management of numerous diseases. The effect of psychological stress on disease severity is particularly striking in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)4, with numerous epidemiological studies supporting the hypothesis that stressful life events can induce exacerbated IBD flares5–8. However, the mechanistic basis for aggravated stressassociated IBD flares is not fully understood. In this study, we uncover several mechanisms by which psychological stress influences bowel inflammation via the enteric nervous system (ENS). Unlike the central nervous Schneider et al. Page 3 Cell. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2024 June 22. Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript

system (CNS), where responses to psychological stress have been deeply characterized9, ENS responses to stress and their consequences are less well understood. We provide insights into how the ENS may serve as a relay between brain-derived stress signals and the priming of inflammatory responses in the intestine. Our findings highlight enteric neurons and glia as possible therapeutic targets to ameliorate inflammatory sequelae of mental health impairment. RESULTS Monocytes mediate stress-driven colitis exacerbation To investigate mechanisms underlying the impact of psychological stress on intestinal inflammation, we used a mouse model of prolonged psychological stress (restraint stress10) and induced colitis using dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) (Figure 1A). Psychological stress exacerbated intestinal inflammation, as documented by weight loss, colonoscopy, mortality, histology, and fecal lipocalin levels (Figures 1B–1E and S1A–S1C). RNA-sequencing of colonic tissue revealed pronounced changes in gene expression induced by psychological stress. This included downregulation of genes involved in type 2 immunity (Il33, Il13ra, Retnla) as well as antimicrobial peptides (Ang4, Itln1, Lyz2). In contrast, the expression of IBD-associated genes (Duox2, Duoxa2) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (Tnf Ccl2, Il6) was upregulated (Figures S1D–S1F). Restraint stress-induced colitis exacerbation was also observed under housing conditions that ameliorate environmental stress, including thermoneutrality11 and cage enrichment (Figures S1G–S1N). Although we noted slightly increased water intake in the stressed group, colitis aggravation was not caused by increased DSS consumption (Figures S1O–S1T). We also observed exacerbated colitis in stressed mice across different starting weights and durations of the stress period (Figures S1U and S1V). Interestingly, when we applied restraint stress at different time points during the experimental protocol (Figure S2A), we noted that stress experienced before the onset of colitis had the strongest effect of disease exacerbation (Figures S2B–S2E), suggesting that psychological stress may precondition the bowel for enhanced inflammation during the subsequent encounter of a colitogenic trigger. Similarly, in an alternative IBD model13 that is based on genetic deficiency in IL-10, restraint stress led to body weight loss, elevated colonoscopy scores, higher rate of rectal prolapses, and reduced colon length (Figures S2J–S2N). Together, these data from several independent mouse models suggest that psychological stress per se is not sufficient to induce overt colitis but preconditions the intestinal mucosa by inducing a pro-inflammatory state that exacerbates the consequences of a colitogenic trigger. Among all clusters, T cells, macrophages/monocytes, and innate lymphoid cells had the most differentially expressed genes in stressed mice (Figure S3C), nominating these cell types as potential drivers of stress-induced enhanced intestinal inflammation. We first focused on T cells, given their well-described role in the pathogenesis of colitis14. Psychological stress induced several elements of an enhanced TH17 response in the intestine (Figures S3D and S3E). However, adaptive immune cells were dispensable for stress-mediated enhancement of colitis (Figures S3F–S3I). We thus turned to innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), motivated by their large number of differentially regulated genes (Figure S3C), the enrichment of IL-22-producing ILCs in the intestines of stressed mice (Figures S4A and S4B), and a recent report on the role for IL-22 in stress-mediated exacerbation of enteric infection15. However, neither genetic deficiency in IL-22 nor neutralization of the IL-22-inducing cytokine IL-23 influenced the stress-mediated colitis phenotype (Figures S4C–S4I). Likewise, ILC-deficient Rag2/Il2rg knockout mice were as susceptible to the impact of stress on colitis as their wild-type counterparts (Figure S4J). These results suggest that neither innate nor adaptive lymphocytes are essential drivers of the intestinal inflammatory response to stress. We therefore focused on myeloid cells, and in particular on monocytes and macrophages, given their strong transcriptional changes induced by psychological stress (Figure S3C). Sub-clustering of the single-cell data revealed five populations of myeloid cells (Figures 1F and S4K): three monocyte (Mono 1, 2 and 3) and two macrophage subsets (Mac 1-2). The impact of psychological stress was particularly apparent in the transcriptomes of the Mono1 and Mac2 clusters (Figure S4L). Notably, pseudotime trajectory analysis indicated an accumulation of monocytes in stressed mice (Figure 1G), which we verified by flow cytometry (Figures 1H–1K). Perception of stress by the CNS results in elevated levels of catecholamines and corticosteroids in the periphery16. Successful chemical sympathectomy was confirmed by strongly reduced norepinephrine concentrations (Figure S5B). Interestingly, abrogation of adrenergic signaling seemed to further exacerbate colitis in stressed mice, as evidenced by pronounced weight loss, high mortality, and severe mucosal damage (Figures S5C–S5G). Likewise, mice treated with the β2-receptor antagonist ICI-118,551 showed an exacerbated stress-induced colitis phenotype (Figures S5H–S5J). Together, these data suggest that catecholamines counteract, rather than enhance, inflammation during chronic stress17–19. To investigate the involvement of increased glucocorticoids in stress-induced severe colitis, we pharmacologically blocked the brain-mediated induction of adrenal corticosterone release with the corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor 1 (CRHR1) antagonist antalarmin. This treatment efficiently diminished corticosterone levels (Figure S5K) and rendered mice resistant to the impact of restraint stress on colitis (Figures S5L–S50). Similarly, corticosterone depletion by adrenalectomy (Figures S5P–S5T) or inhibition of glucocorticoid receptor (GR) signaling using mifepristone (RU-486) prevented colitis exacerbation by psychological stress (Figures 2B–2D), suggesting that glucocorticoids mediated the detrimental effect of stress on gut inflammation. Since RU-486 is not specific to GR, but also targets the progesterone receptor, we wondered whether GR signaling was sufficient to recapitulate the effect of stress on colitis. Remarkably, Nr3c1Hand2 mice were protected from the impact of stress on colitis (Figures 3A–3F), without affecting food or water intake (Figures S6E and S6F). We observed the same protective effect of GR deficiency in the ENS when we induced colitis with an IL-10 receptor-targeting antibody (Figures S6G–S6L). Given that Nr3c1Hand2 mice lack GR expression in both enteric neurons and glia, we sought to disentangle the individual roles of glia and neurons in the gastrointestinal tract. The large majority of adult enteric glia are characterized by Plp1 or Sox10 expression24. We thus generated inducible Nr3c1Plp1/Sox10 mice and exposed them to restraint stress. Notably, deletion of GR in adult glia largely protected mice from the colitis-exacerbating effects of stress (Figures 3H–3K). Collectively, these results point to the ENS, and particularly enteric glia cells, as a critical relay between glucocorticoids derived from the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and inflammatory reactions in the gut. The expression profile of eGAPS was characterized by the induction of pro-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic pathways, while adhesion and cellular interaction pathways were downregulated (Figure S7C). Specifically, eGAPS were marked by high expression of the glucocorticoid-induced factors Nr4a1, Nr4a2, and Nr4a3, the ubiquitin ligase Arih1, the apoptosis/necroptosis mediator Ripk1, and the transcription factor Stat3 (Figures 3N and S7D). DISCUSSION Chronic psychological stress is strongly associated with the severity of IBD flares6,8,35, but the underlying mechanisms remain largely unclear. In this study, we identify a cascade of cellular and molecular events that link stress perception to exacerbation of enteric inflammation, elements of which may apply to other inflammatory diseases of the gut as well as extraintestinal disorders associated with psychological stress. Our findings have several important implications. First, we provide important insights into the biology of enteric glia cells. Our results demonstrate that the molecular state of enteric glia and their impact on the intestinal microenvironment are influenced by CNS-derived signals. As such, enteric glia may perform previously unrecognized functions in CNSENS communication. Our results demonstrate that the molecular state of enteric glia and their impact on the intestinal microenvironment are influenced by CNS-derived signals. As such, enteric glia may perform previously unrecognized functions in CNSENS communication. Of note, the molecular profile of stress-associated astrocytes shares several features with eGAPS, including high expression levels of Nur family transcription factors36,37, suggesting that this stress-associated glial expression profile may emerge via common signaling mechanisms in different tissues. Second, our study addresses a conundrum that arises from the fact that stress worsens inflammatory disease, while the canonical systemic mediators of psychological stress, catecholamines and glucocorticoids, are generally considered anti-inflammatory16. The induction of inflammatory enteric glia and exacerbated colitis by glucocorticoid signaling was particularly perplexing, given that the glucocorticoid receptor agonist prednisone is used to treat colitis in IBD patients. There are several possible explanations for this paradox. For instance, prolonged stress or dexamethasone treatment may induce inadequate adrenal production of corticosterone due to negative feedback-mediated suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis38,39. However, the beneficial effects of acute GR inhibition (Figures 2B–2D) are not consistent with “adrenal suppression”. Alternatively, the balance between anti- and pro-inflammatory effects of glucocorticoids might be a temporal phenomenon40–42. Similarly, clinical observations have documented that only short-term steroid treatment leads to beneficial outcomes in IBD44,45. Third, our study emphasizes the importance of considering a patient’s mental health in the clinical management of inflammatory diseases. Given that we found opposing roles of two common IBD treatment regimens (corticosteroids and monoclonal antibodies against TNF) on the severity of stress-mediated colitis in mice, it is possible that treatment effects vary depending on the psychological state of affected individuals. The evaluation of mental state, in conjunction with strategies to reduce stress, anxiety, and depression, could thus be a powerful and underutilized tool to enhance treatment success46. Limitations of this study Our model implies that glia are the critical source of CSF1 and neurons the critical source of TGFβ2 in stress-exacerbated colitis. While several lines of evidence support this model, the generation of new conditional knockout mice for cell type-specific ablation of these cytokines will be required for unequivocal evidence. Additionally, our findings do not clarify the temporal sequence of events underlying TGFβ2-mediated neuronal alterations in response to stress. Is TGFβ2 induced by GR signaling and subsequently reprograms neurons to express precursor genes rather than differentiation genes? Alternatively, does GR signaling induce an immature state in neurons that is then propagated by TGFβ2? Similar questions regarding the induction of the eGAPS phenotype remain to be clarified. Our model suggests that the downstream effect of glial and neuronal perturbation by psychological stress are largely distinct, with glia affecting TNF-driven inflammation and neuronal changes driving dysmotility. However, inhibition of TGFβ signaling also provides a certain degree of protection from severe inflammation, albeit only partially. However, inhibition of TGFβ signaling also provides a certain degree of protection from severe inflammation, albeit only partially. This either suggests that our dichotomous model is oversimplified, or that the rescue of motility itself helps to ameliorate bowel inflammation. Finally, our study does not address the evolutionary purpose of exacerbated inflammatory responses to chronic stress. Systemic stress responses likely serve the function of resource allocation during times of high energy demand. Notably, the relative benefits of a heightened inflammatory and alert state versus an immunosuppressed state that allows for reallocation of energy within the organism may depend on the source and nature of the stressful trigger47. We speculate that glucocorticoids thus serve a dual function, with acute immunosuppression purposed to centralize resources for survival of essential organs, followed by inflammatory states in the periphery in case the trigger persists. NicheNet Ligand-Receptor Analysis—Ligand-receptor analysis was performed using NicheNet (v. 1.0.0), a method that predicts which ligands in a ‘sender cell’ population regulate gene expression in a ‘receiver’ population. NicheNet was the preferred method for ligand-receptor analysis, as it predicts which ligands influence gene expression in other cells and what target genes are affected by each ligand. It does this by first prioritizing ligands based on how well a ligand can predict observed differentially expressed genes in the receiver population. It then infers active-ligand target links to see which prioritized ligands regulate which differentially expressed genes in the receiver cells. This goes beyond other models that solely predict ligand-receptor interactions where specific gene targets are not considered. Analysis Pipeline.: To perform NicheNet analysis, sender (eGAPS) and receiver (Mono1, Mono2, Mac1, Mac2) populations were defined. A geneset of interest was also defined, which are genes in the receiver population that may be affected by ligands in the senders. Here, the geneset of interest was defined as differentially expressed genes between stressed and control conditions in the receiver populations. Differentially expressed genes between control and stress (adjusted p-value < 0.05) were determined using Seurat (v. 3.2.2). Background genes were defined as any genes that were not differentially expressed. NicheNet network gene symbols were also converted from human to mouse. NicheNet first defined a set of potential ligands, which are ligands that are expressed by the sender cell population and bind to a putative receptor expressed by the target population. NicheNet first defined a set of potential ligands, which are ligands that are expressed by the sender cell population and bind to a putative receptor expressed by the target population. Ligandactivity analysis was then performed, which ranked the previously defined potential ligands based on their level of regulation of genes in the geneset of interest compared to the background gene set. Pearson correlation was used to determine ligand activity; calculated coefficients were between the ligand’s target predictions and the observed transcriptional response. As there was overlap in terms of which cell types expressed which ligands/ receptors, ligands, and receptors were assigned to their respective cell types by observing which cell types expressed the respective ligand/receptor to a degree that was higher than the average plus the standard deviation. Active ligand target links (receptors and genes targeted by top-ranked ligands) were then determined. Visualization Pipeline.: CircosPlot (from Circlize package v. 0.4.13) was used to display the most significant ligand-target links, links comprising the bottom 95% of lowest regulatory potential scores were removed. Each segment of ligands and targets was given a specific color and order and gaps were defined between the different segments. Links were made transparent based on ligand-target potential score; the lower the score, the more transparent the link. Widjaja Inflammatory Bowel Disease Institute, Cedars Sinai Medical Center, Los Angeles, California, USA 11Hospital da Luz, Lisboa, Portugal Abstract Objective: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is characterized by dysbiosis, but it remains unclear to what extent dysbiosis develops in unaffected at-risk individuals. To address this, we investigated age-related patterns of fecal and serum markers of dysbiosis in high-risk multiplex IBD families (2 or more affected first-degree relatives). Design: Fecal and serum samples were collected from multiplex IBD and control families (95 IBD, 292 unaffected, 51 controls). Findings were validated in independent cohorts of 616 and 1,173 subjects including patients with IBD, infants born to mothers with IBD, and controls. 16S rRNA gene sequencing and global untargeted metabolomics profiling of feces and serum were performed. Results: Microbial and metabolomic parameters of dysbiosis progressively decreased from infancy until age 8. This microbial maturation process was slower in infants born to mothers with IBD. After age 15, dysbiosis steadily increased in unaffected relatives throughout adulthood. Dysbiosis was accompanied by marked shifts in the fecal metabolome and, to a lesser extent, the serum metabolome. Fecal and serum metabolomics dysbiosis indices validated in an independent cohort. Dysbiosis was associated with elevated anti-microbial serologies but not with fecal calprotectin. Dysbiosis metrics differentiated IBD from non-IBD comparably to serologies, with a model combining calprotectin, fecal metabolomics dysbiosis index, and serology score demonstrating highest accuracy. Conclusion: These findings support that dysbiosis exists as a pre-disease state detectable by fecal and serum

metabolomics dysbiosis indices validated in an independent cohort. Dysbiosis was associated with elevated anti-microbial serologies but not with fecal calprotectin. Dysbiosis metrics differentiated IBD from non-IBD comparably to serologies, with a model combining calprotectin, fecal metabolomics dysbiosis index, and serology score demonstrating highest accuracy. Conclusion: These findings support that dysbiosis exists as a pre-disease state detectable by fecal and serum biomarkers for IBD risk prediction. Given expansion of disease-modifying agents and non-invasive imaging, the indices developed here may facilitate earlier diagnoses and improved management in at-risk individuals. attributed to multiple environmental risk factors including diet, urban living, and antibiotic usage interacting with underlying genetic risk from over 200 IBD-associated loci.2 It is widely believed that the intestinal microbiome is a critical mediator of the relationship of environmental and genetic risk factors with disease induction. This has been supported by the preponderance of IBD-associated genes involved in host-microbiome interactions and extensive preclinical research demonstrating that the microbiota can alter susceptibility to experimental models of IBD.3 Prevailing models of IBD pathogenesis posit that there is a microbial risk state – often referred to as “dysbiosis” – that precedes the onset of intestinal inflammation and predisposes to its development due to a combination of reduced anti-inflammatory homeostatic signals and pathobiont potential within the microbial community.4 Human microbiome association studies have consistently shown alterations in microbial composition and function in IBD patients, including at the time of disease diagnosis and during endoscopic remission.5 6 However, it has been unclear to what extent observed microbial profiles in clinically diagnosed IBD patients are a cause of disease rather than representing a consequence of prior or ongoing intestinal inflammation. To investigate whether dysbiosis occurs in those at high risk for IBD, studies have characterized the microbiome of unaffected first-degree relatives (FDRs). In an early study, we studied microbial composition of 21 pediatric IBD patients and their 69 FDRs.7 We found by modeling microbial community structure that the microbiome of individuals in this cohort could be classified into two community states, termed OTU-types. The OTUtype with lower microbial diversity – consistent with a state of dysbiosis – was strongly associated with IBD but was also found in some unaffected FDRs, raising the possibility that it represented a pre-disease state. The OTUtype with lower microbial diversity – consistent with a state of dysbiosis – was strongly associated with IBD but was also found in some unaffected FDRs, raising the possibility that it represented a pre-disease state. Recent data from the GEM study of unaffected FDRs of patients with Crohn’s disease (CD) support that microbial changes can precede CD onset.8 A microbiome risk score generated by machine learning from genus-level composition in samples obtained within approximately 3 years prior to diagnosis was associated with increased risk of developing CD. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that pre-disease microbial changes promote risk for subsequent disease development, though it remains possible that the reported signature taxa were markers of a subclinical early disease phase. To further define putative pre-disease dysbiosis in those at high risk for IBD, we performed a multi-omics analysis of microbial composition and function – including both fecal and serum global untargeted metabolomics – in a large cohort of Ashkenazi Jewish families with a history of multiplex IBD. We also assessed predictors of future IBD risk including anti-microbial serologic biomarkers and intestinal inflammation as assessed by fecal calprotectin.8 9 Building on the previously reported microbial community states defined as OTU-types, we characterized an IBD-associated dysbiosis that had parallels with early life microbial maturation, appeared in unaffected family members during early adulthood, was associated with elevated anti-microbial serologies, and could be accurately predicted by fecal and serum metabolite markers. MATERIALS AND METHODS Ashkenazi Jewish families with a history of multiplex IBD (2 or more affected first-degree relatives, including twins) and control (no known family history of IBD) Ashkenazi Jewish families were recruited from the greater New York metropolitan area by a combination of outreach to community leaders, posted fliers, and a series of educational and recruitment events in the communities. Stool was collected at home and sent by overnight shipping on ice packs to the research team. Blood samples were drawn from participants over age 7, and buccal swabs were obtained for those under 7. Longitudinal monitoring is ongoing to detect incident IBD cases. The study was approved by the Mount Sinai IRB (STUDY-16–00021). Validation was performed using the previously described MECONIUM and MSCCR cohorts.10 11 Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing, fecal calprotectin, fecal and serum global untargeted metabolomics, serologies, and polygenic risk score along with bioinformatics analysis are described in the Supplementary Materials. Community members were involved in study design and conduct. Research questions reflected their interest in understanding factors that increase their risk of IBD. Study protocols were optimized with community input to minimize participant burden. Metabolomics profiles were significantly associated with IBD status and partially separated IBD patients from unaffected family members and controls over age 3, mirroring the pattern seen with microbiome composition (Fig. 3A–B, S11). Given the similarity between the fecal metabolome and microbiome, the two datasets were directly compared by Procrustes superimposition and found to be highly correlated (Mantel r=0.67, p<10−5) (Fig. 3C). This supported that microbial community structure as represented by OTU-types could be a driver of metabolomic differences. Indeed, metabolomics profiles were more strongly associated with OTU-type than IBD group or fecal calprotectin (Fig. 3B). Short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were then analyzed and found to be depleted in IBD, with significant reduction in all eight measured SCFAs in UC/IBDU and in hexanoate and valerate in CD (Fig. 3D, Fig. S12A–B). Dysbiosis is associated with increased anti-microbial serologies It has previously been reported that increased levels of anti-microbial serologies predict future risk of IBD.9 To assess for a relationship of dysbiosis with serologic responses, we measured levels of Cbir1 (anti-flagellin), OmpC (outer membrane protein of E. coli), IgA and IgG ASCA (anti-Saccharomyces), and ANCA. All five serologies were significantly higher in CD and UC/IBDU than unaffected relatives and controls, which did not significantly differ (Fig. S18A). Logistic regression models were created to differentiate IBD from unaffected family members based upon fecal calprotectin, serology score, and dysbiosis metrics. Fecal calprotectin had relatively poor discriminative ability with AUC 0.67 whereas serology score was more robust with AUC 0.86. Dysbiosis score and fecal metabolomics dysbiosis index had comparable accuracy as serology score with AUC 0.84 and 0.86, while serum metabolomics dysbiosis index had somewhat less accuracy with AUC 0.76 (Fig. 6A). A combined fecal classifier with fecal calprotectin, dysbiosis score, and fecal metabolomics dysbiosis index achieved AUC 0.87 with fecal metabolomics dysbiosis index contributing the most to the regression model and no significant additional contribution of dysbiosis score (Fig. 6B). DISCUSSION We defined a multi-omics compositional and functional signature of dysbiosis in multiplex IBD families. Dysbiosis emerged in this cohort in late adolescence to early adulthood, overlapping with the median age of IBD onset in our cohort (19 years of age) and the reported age range of peak IBD incidence.12 The majority of IBD patients had dysbiosis, but its onset in unaffected members of some multiplex IBD families likely did not reflect a subclinical mucosal inflammatory process as there was no relationship with fecal calprotectin. Among unaffected family members, dysbiosis was associated with elevated Jacobs et al. Page 8 Gut. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2025 November 11. levels of serologic markers of immune response against microbial antigens, a known predisease indicator.9 However, dysbiosis may not be a driver of serologic profiles in IBD by itself, as a study of circulating antibody repertoires of IBD patients did not find any associations with fecal microbiota.13 Instead, dysbiosis within multiplex IBD families likely signifies increased likelihood not just of IBD but also its pre-disease stages including development of anti-microbial serologies. Supporting the potential utility of dysbiosis as an indicator of a pre-IBD susceptibility state, models incorporating dysbiosis metrics predicted high risk in two out of three initial incident IBD cases. It is unknown what could explain the onset of dysbiosis in late adolescence, as microbial changes during adolescence have received little study compared to those in early life. Longitudinal changes in microbiome have been reported following puberty; however, dysbiosis was not detected in the family cohort until after age 15, past the typical age of pubertal onset.14 Development of dysbiosis may reflect changes that occur during the late adolescence to young adulthood transition, including dietary alteration, initiation of smoking, altered sleep patterns, increased stress, chronic antibiotic exposure for conditions such as acne, and other lifestyle shifts as individuals gain greater autonomy and leave their family homes.15 In support of this, a longitudinal study of students during their freshman year of college demonstrated significant shifts in microbial composition.16 We further found that dysbiosis became more prevalent with increasing age. This may reflect the cumulative effect of environmental exposures over time resulting in progressive dysbiosis throughout adulthood. This does not appear related to underlying genetic risk given the lack of association with IBD-related variants summarized by polygenic risk score. Control Ashkenazi families in RTP as well as the adult controls in the two validation cohorts also showed increasing dysbiosis with age, suggesting

Control Ashkenazi families in RTP as well as the adult controls in the two validation cohorts also showed increasing dysbiosis with age, suggesting that factors driving dysbiosis are common and that dysbiosis alone is insufficient to induce IBD. Prior studies have reported that age is a significant factor explaining variation in microbial composition across adult populations.17 Interestingly, some of the taxa that are depleted with dysbiosis have also been reported to be consistently depleted with increased age, including Faecalibacterium and Roseburia.18 Surprisingly, there was a clear relationship of dysbiosis metrics with early life microbial maturation. Dysbiosis in later life may parallel a disordered microbiome in early life that has not matured to a stable adult-like state. Intriguingly, children of mothers with IBD were found to have delays in attainment of a healthy microbial community state as assessed by OTU-types as well as dysbiosis score. This delay in microbial maturation is consistent with earlier reports from MECONIUM that infants of mothers with IBD have lower diversity microbiota than controls.10 It is unknown whether delayed microbial maturation confers increased likelihood of developing dysbiosis in early adulthood and may therefore contribute to IBD risk in offspring of mothers with IBD.19 This would be an important area of future study as it raises the possibility that dysbiosis risk in adulthood could be modulated by microbiome interventions in early life. enrichment of cholate and its conjugates, depletion of the secondary bile acid lithocholate, and enrichment of acyl carnitines.20 Tryptophan and its metabolites were also notably associated with dysbiosis. Many microbial-derived tryptophan catabolites are agonists of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (Ahr), which modulates mucosal immune function.21 A pattern of increased kynurenine and decreased Ahr ligands has been reported in IBD and may promote vulnerability to intestinal inflammation.22 Among the SCFAs, dysbiosis was associated specifically with reduction in butyrate but not acetate or propionate. Butyrate is known to have wide-ranging anti-inflammatory effects that reduce severity of experimental IBD models, supporting that dysbiosis favors increased inflammatory tone.23 There was also prominent alteration in phenolic compounds, which arise from microbial metabolism and were recently found to also be altered in irritable bowel syndrome patients.24 Serum metabolites similarly showed a highly significant relationship with dysbiosis, with concordant changes in the fecal and serum metabolome of known bacterial products – including phenolic compounds and bile acids – supporting that serum levels directly reflected intestinal microbial metabolism. Strengths of this study included the unique risk profiles of multiplex IBD families, multiomics approach including paired fecal and serum metabolomics, large sample size with two validation cohorts, and integration of dysbiosis measures into risk models with other known pre-disease markers. A current limitation is the small number of incident IBD cases; continued longitudinal follow-up is ongoing and increased numbers of incident cases in the future would allow further validation of the relationship of dysbiosis defined by microbial and metabolite markers to IBD risk. Another limitation is the comparatively small number of control families, reducing power to detect differences in dysbiosis between unaffected family members and controls. Moreover, the generalizability of findings from the RTP cohort to other at-risk IBD populations may be questioned; importantly, the fecal and serum dysbiosis

of the relationship of dysbiosis defined by microbial and metabolite markers to IBD risk. Another limitation is the comparatively small number of control families, reducing power to detect differences in dysbiosis between unaffected family members and controls. Moreover, the generalizability of findings from the RTP cohort to other at-risk IBD populations may be questioned; importantly, the fecal and serum dysbiosis metrics were applicable to the mixed ethnicity MECONIUM and MSCCR cohorts. In conclusion, we demonstrated that dysbiosis is detectable in at-risk unaffected individuals from multiplex IBD families starting in late adolescence and becomes increasingly prevalent throughout adulthood. We further established the feasibility of both stool and blood-based microbial metabolite measurement to assess for dysbiosis in at-risk populations. This will require longitudinal validation but raises the prospect of prospectively identifying microbially at-risk individuals who may benefit from microbiota-targeted interventions and non-invasive imaging for early disease detection. Reproducible characterization of microbial community features that are consistent with dysbiosis will also promote preclinical studies to characterize specific microbes and their products within dysbiotic microbial communities that increase IBD susceptibility. This makes it feasible to identify prophylactic targets for IBD prevention as well as biomarkers of risk, bringing us further along down the road to prevention of IBD after decades of rising incidence worldwide. What is already known on this topic: • While dysbiosis is accepted as a notable feature of IBD, it’s unclear to what extent IBD-associated dysbiosis occurs in the absence of disease in those at risk. What this study adds: • Dysbiosis was detected in unaffected individuals from multiplex IBD families starting in late adolescence and was associated with fecal and serum metabolite profiles. • Early life maturation could be captured by dysbiosis metrics and was delayed in infants of mothers with IBD. • Dysbiosis in unaffected members of multiplex IBD families was associated with elevated anti-microbial serologies and could be incorporated into fecal or serum biomarker risk models for IBD. How this study might affect research, practice or policy: • Patterns of intestinal dysbiosis in unaffected members of multiplex IBD families suggest that it is insufficient to induce IBD but may represent a pre-disease susceptibility state that promotes disease onset in those with underlying risk. • It may be feasible to prospectively identify microbially at-risk individuals who could benefit from microbiota-targeted interventions. Abstract Background: Defining immune dysregulation during the asymptomatic prodrome of immunemediated diseases offers opportunities for early disease detection and interception. In inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), prodromal immune changes remain poorly characterized. Objective: To define pre-clinical immunological alterations by characterizing longitudinal serum antibody repertoires using high-throughput phage-display immunoprecipitation sequencing (PhIPSeq). Design: We applied PhIP-Seq to profile antibody responses in 2,000 longitudinal serum samples from 200 individuals who developed Crohn’s disease (CD), 200 who developed ulcerative colitis (UC), and 100 matched healthy controls (HCs) within the US military PREDICTS cohort, collected up to 10 years before diagnosis. Antibody repertoires were profiled against 357,000 microbial-, viral-, food-, and immune-associated peptides. Results: Antibody repertoire variability was increased up to ~4 years pre-diagnosis in pre-CD and pre-UC individuals. Differential analyses revealed elevated herpesvirus-directed responses (notably Epstein-Barr virus) and anti-flagellin antibodies up to 10 years pre-diagnosis in CD, particularly in individuals who later developed complicated or ileal disease. In contrast, responses to encapsulated bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus, Neisseria) progressively declined towards diagnosis. Pre-UC was characterized by combined antimicrobial, antiviral, and autoantibody signatures,

Conclusion: Large-scale serological profiling of archived pre-diagnostic samples identified disease-specific immune trajectories years before IBD onset, providing novel insights into disease pathogenesis in its prodromal phase. Keywords Inflammatory bowel disease; antibodies; antibody repertoires; diagnosis; pre-diagnostics Introduction Chronic immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) such as inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs), encompassing Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), are believed to arise from a prolonged prodromal phase, during which immunological alterations accumulate years before clinical onset [1–4]. In this phase, disease-specific humoral immune responses have been reported, including anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA) and anti-flagellin antibodies (e.g., anti-Fla-X, anti-A4-Fla2) preceding CD, and perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA) or anti-αvβ6 antibodies preceding UC [3,5–10]. However, conventional assays capture only a narrow spectrum of antibody reactivities against pre-defined antigens, limiting insights into the breadth and dynamics of immune responses during disease development [11,12]. Phage-display immunoprecipitation sequencing (PhIP-Seq) enables massively parallel profiling of antibody repertoires against hundreds of thousands of peptides, spanning microbial, viral, and host-derived antigens [13–15]. This approach has been successfully applied to the microbiome [16] and to diverse disease contexts, including viral infections [17,18], autoimmune diseases [19–21], and IBD [22,23]. By interrogating immune responses at unprecedented scale, PhIP-Seq provides a powerful platform to delineate disease prodromes and immune trajectories. It has also provided insights into Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) immunity and its role in immune-mediated diseases [19,20,24]. Herein, we leverage PhIP-Seq in a large pre-diagnostic cohort – the PREDICTS (Proteomic Evaluation and Discovery in an IBD Cohort of Tri-service Subjects) cohort [25], comprising thousands of longitudinal serum samples collected up to a decade prior to diagnosis. Using IBD as a model, we identify antibody signatures that precede clinical onset and characterize their persistence and temporal trajectories. Our findings illustrate that large-scale serological profiling in pre-diagnostic IBD biobanks can illuminate prodromal immune alterations. Materials and Methods

Using the Defense Medical Surveillance System (DMSS), new-onset cases of CD and UC were identified in the period of 1998–2013, which were defined as having two or more medical encounters with the International Classification of Diseases (ICD, 9th Revision, Clinical Modification – ICD-9-CM, https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/icd/ icd9cm.htm, Accessed June 24, 2024) code for CD and UC (555.0, 555.1, and 555.9 for CD and 556 for UC, including all subgroup codes for both, which were linked to the DoDSR). Case identification followed the previously published PREDICTS/DMSS algorithm [25], requiring ≥2 IBD-coded medical encounters (to reduce misclassification based on single administrative entries) and ≥1 medical encounter with a CPT code for a lower gastrointestinal endoscopic procedure preceding or accompanying an IBD-coded encounter. The use of ≥2 ICD-9-CM codes as a case definition for IBD has previously been validated in military and other administrative databases, demonstrating positive predictive values of approximately 80–90% for Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis [26–28]. Prior PREDICTS analyses additionally showed no significant differences in gastrointestinal-related ICD-9 coding between cases and controls in the two years preceding the index diagnosis date, supporting the validity of incident case identification [3]. PhIP-Seq procedures Design and content of the antigen libraries: Details on the design, content, antigen processing, and cloning of the PhIP-Seq libraries can be found in the Supplementary Methods. Three antigen libraries covering a total of 357,000 different antigens (Fig. 1B) were used in this study: a 244,000-variant library (“agilent”) [16], a 100,000-variant library (“twist”) [29], and a 13,000-variant coronavirus library (“corona2”) [30]. The 244,000-variant library encompasses a wide array of microbial antigens derived from 28,668 different proteins, including 27,837 proteins from microbiota antigens. It features antigens from various sources: bacterial genes (122,551 peptides, ~50%) and strains (24,510 peptides, ~10%) of commensal bacteria selected from metagenomic sequencing data of nearly 1,000 healthy individuals [31], selected pathogenic bacteria (24,500 peptides, ~10%) [16], probiotic bacteria (14,700 peptides, ~6%) [32], known antibody-coated bacteria (22,050 peptides, ~9%) [33], virulence factor antigens (24,164 peptides, ~10%) from the virulence factor database (VFDB) [34], and a set of biological and technical controls (11,525 peptides, ~5%, see [16] for details). In addition to these standard subgroups, a custom subgroup of flagellin peptides was also created

(24,500 peptides, ~10%) [16], probiotic bacteria (14,700 peptides, ~6%) [32], known antibody-coated bacteria (22,050 peptides, ~9%) [33], virulence factor antigens (24,164 peptides, ~10%) from the virulence factor database (VFDB) [34], and a set of biological and technical controls (11,525 peptides, ~5%, see [16] for details). In addition to these standard subgroups, a custom subgroup of flagellin peptides was also created based on a previously published annotation [35]. The 100,000-variant library comprises antigens from bacteriophages (~40,000 peptides, selected from those infecting commensal bacteria, probiotic bacteria, and pathogenic bacteria) [29], allergens from six different allergen databases (~30,000 peptides) [36–41], and all B cell antigens as deposited in the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) on January 14th, 2018, except for non-human host, allergens (which were taken separately), and Chagas disease epitopes (~30,000 peptides) [42]. Allergen peptides were derived from the IEDB list [41], the WHO/IUIS Allergen Nomenclature Database (www.allergen.org) [36], AllergenOnline (www.allergenonline.org) [37], Allergome (www.allergome.org) [38], the Database of allergen families, AllFam (www.meduniwien.ac.at/allfam/) [39], the Structural Database of Allergenic Proteins (SDAP) (femi.utmb.edu) [40], and from allergenic helminthic proteins [41]. The 13,000-variant coronavirus-focused library was created following the COVID-19 pandemic and contains antigens from both seasonal/common cold human and animal coronaviruses. Further details on the creation of this antigen library can be found in [30]. For all antigen libraries, antigens were rationally selected by prioritizing previously reported bacterial antigens and strains that are known to be recognized by the immune system as well as uncharacterized antigens. Here, the focus was primarily put on their functions, particularly those with a high likelihood of being exposed to the immune system, such as membrane-, surface-, motility-, and secreted proteins (see [16] for details). Antigen selection was conducted without considering peptide sequence length, necessitating peptide splitting within the given 230 nt limit of DNA oligonucleotide synthesis. Further details on the antigen library composition and antigen selection process can be found elsewhere [16]. Immunoprecipitation and next-generation sequencing: Experimental details of the immunoprecipitation (IP) and next-generation sequencing (NGS) steps can be found in the Supplementary Methods. Antibody testing using a commercially available panel (Prometheus Panel): Each serum sample analyzed for this study was also previously tested [3] for a specified panel of circulating serological antibodies, including anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA, both IgG and IgA), perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA), anti-Escherichia coli outer membrane porin C (anti-OmpC), and three distinct anti-flagellin antibodies (anti-CBir1, anti-Fla-X, and anti-A4-Fla2). These antibodies were measured using commercially available ELISAs performed at Prometheus Laboratories (San Diego, CA, USA). PhIP-Seq data: Raw sequencing reads obtained from NGS after IP were reduced to 1.25 million identifiable reads per sample, only capturing those within one error of all possible barcodes for which the paired-end matched the identifiable antibody-bound peptide. For data analysis, at least 750,000 reads were required in case fewer reads were obtained. Antigen enrichment was calculated through comparing the total number of reads per antigen with the input read numbers, which were determined when the phage library was sequenced before IP. Each input read number per sample was assumed to generate an output read number null distribution that was fitted using a generalized Poisson distribution. Parameters were estimated separately for each input read number in each sample, and scores were subsequently generated by fitting the parameters to three distribution parameters for all samples, followed by interpolation for each input read number [14]. Fold changes were calculated as the number of reads for antibody-bound peptides (after IP) vs. the number of input reads (prior to IP), computed only for significantly enriched antibody-bound peptides (which were referred to as seropositive antibodies), while the remaining peptides were set to zero. Additionally, fold changes were calculated only with a minimum of 25 input reads per peptide. Baseline sequencing of the antigen phage library (prior to IP) was conducted at >100-fold coverage. Samples with fewer than 200 significantly enriched antigens compared to input reads were excluded. For most statistical Bourgonje et al. Page 6 Gut. General statistical analyses: Baseline descriptive statistics of the study cohort were presented as means ± standard deviation (SD), medians with interquartile range [IQR] or as proportions with corresponding percentages (%). Normality was assessed through visual inspection of normal probability (Q-Q) plots and histograms. Differences across groups were tested using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with post-hoc tests or nonparametrically using Kruskal-Wallis tests with post-hoc Mann-Whitney U-tests, as appropriate. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed for dimensionality reduction purposes and to identify potential determinants of data clustering. Overall antibody diversity across samples was determined through calculating the Shannon diversity index/alpha-diversity, based on the number of antibody-bound peptides significantly bound. For longitudinal analysis of antibody-bound peptide counts across repeated sampling timepoints, global differences were first assessed using Friedman tests, followed by pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction for multiple testing. Longitudinal stability of antibody repertoires across the different study timepoints was analyzed through calculating point-biserial or phi (φ)-coefficients or mean square contingency coefficients, which are suitable for analyzing correlations between binary variables. To analyze longitudinal changes in frequencies of antibody repertoires over time, generalized linear mixed-effects models with logit-link function were utilized to account for repeated measurements by applying random effects over individual subjects and to enable testing for interactions between study groups and timepoints. For case-control analyses, which were performed to identify differentially abundant antibody-bound peptides across groups at each study timepoint, logistic regression analysis with covariate adjustment was performed with consistent adjustment for the effects of age and sex. and timepoints. For case-control analyses, which were performed to identify differentially abundant antibody-bound peptides across groups at each study timepoint, logistic regression analysis with covariate adjustment was performed with consistent adjustment for the effects of age and sex. For all longitudinal and cross-sectional analyses, we analyzed data both on the level of individual antibody-bound peptides and on the level of antigen subgroups, for which a taxonomical classification dictionary was used based on at least 5 peptides that occurred within 5–95% of samples within a given analysis (see Table S86). For selected structural analysis of antibody-bound peptides, we performed multiple sequence alignments aiming to identify potentially shared motifs, using MEGA software with the multiple sequence comparison by log-expectation (MUSCLE) algorithm in default settings [43]. Discussion This study delineates a previously underappreciated landscape of serological responses to microbial and non-microbial antigens up to a decade before IBD diagnosis. Longitudinal analysis of 200 pre-CD, 200 pre-UC, and 100 HC individuals over approximately 10 years revealed relatively stable antibody repertoires throughout most of the pre-diagnostic phase, with increased variability closer to diagnosis. Further, we observed striking differences in antibody responses among individuals who developed CD or UC compared with matched HCs, characterized by elevated reactivity to herpesviruses (particularly EBV, CMV, and HSV-1/2) and specific bacterial antigens (e.g., S. aureus) closer to diagnosis. In contrast, reactivity to certain potentially pathogenic, often encapsulated bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus, Haemophilus, Neisseria) and viruses (e.g., rhinoviruses) decreased during the pre-diagnostic phase. Importantly, these data illustrate the power of massively parallel serological profiling to uncover dynamic immune trajectories years before disease onset, highlighting the potential of this approach for studying prodromal immune alterations in IBD and potentially other immune-mediated conditions. Notably, most of our key findings were already detectable at the earliest pre-diagnostic timepoint (~10 years before diagnosis), which strongly argues against peri-diagnostic or post-diagnostic effects driving the observed signals. Elevated EBV-directed antibodies formed one of the strongest pre-diagnostic signatures for individuals who later developed CD, particularly those who developed ileal and complicated disease, detectable up to ~10 years before diagnosis. A recent PhIP-Seq-based study identified a predictive MS signature comprising a cluster of antibodies with motifs resembling a variety of human pathogens, including EBV [19]. The role of EBV reactivity in MS is well-documented, supported by extensive epidemiological data [20], and is gaining recognition for its potential involvement in IBD pathogenesis, possibly through mechanisms such as molecular mimicry or loss of B cell tolerance. Severe EBV infections have been associated with an increased risk of developing IBD later in life [47], and EBV exposure was enriched in both pre- and post-diagnostic cohorts of patients with CD [24]. While the mechanisms linking anti-EBV antibodies to CD onset remain elusive, several hypotheses warrant testing. First, EBV may trigger autoantibody production via molecular mimicry, analogous to MS [48,49]. Recent studies have identified neutralizing autoantibodies against IL-10 in IBD [50], potentially triggered by viral IL-10 expression through mimicry [51]. Additionally, EBV may enhance mutagenesis in B cells, amplifying the production of antibodies reactive to microbiota or self-antigens, which may contribute to disease development. Another possibility is that EBV transcription factors, such as EBNA-2, interact with disease-associated genetic loci, modifying gene transcription. Beyond EBV, individuals who developed CD also exhibited pre-diagnostic overrepresentation of antibody responses against other herpesviruses, including CMV and HSV-1/2, suggesting a broader role for herpesviruses in immune activation during IBD development. These findings reinforce the notion that longitudinal, unbiased serological profiling not only validates previously suspected associations (e.g., EBV in MS), but also uncovers novel, diseasespecific patterns, thereby providing a framework to investigate disease-specific immune mechanisms and to facilitate comparisons across different disease contexts. These highly overrepresented anti-flagellin antibodies were predominantly directed against Lachnospiraceae and were strongly associated with complicated CD at diagnosis. In individuals who developed CD and UC, antibody responses against antigens from potentially pathogenic, often encapsulated, bacteria, including Streptococcus (e.g., surface protein A), Neisseria (e.g., IgA1 protease), and Haemophilus (e.g., heme/hemopexin-binding protein HxuA) declined progressively towards diagnosis. This trend aligns with observations in patients with longstanding IBD [22] and suggests an impaired ability to mount immune responses against encapsulated bacteria, potentially reflecting broader immune dysregulation associated with increasing inflammation and/or disrupted immune tolerance in individuals developing IBD. In contrast to prior work [3,5,10], the diagnosis of UC is preceded by a combination of antimicrobial, antiviral, and autoantibody signatures that included antibodies against a range of antigens, such as antimicrobial antibodies directed to Streptococcus (e.g., surface protein A), Bacteroidales (e.g., peptidase C10 from Paraprevotella), Staphylococcus (e.g., lipase 2), as well as antiviral and autoantibodies. Notably, we observed escalating trajectories of antibodies against MADD protein closer to UC diagnosis. MADD plays a key role in regulating inflammatory responses through the activation of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs) [53]. Dysregulation of MADD could lead to impaired lymphocyte cytotoxicity, as has been reported in case of complete MADD deficiency [54]. Prediagnostic autoantibodies against MADD may serve as a novel biomarker for pre-diagnostic UC. The main strengths of this study pertain to the unique features of our study cohort, including its longitudinal design with multiple pre-diagnostic samples, the inclusion of an age-, sex-, race-, and timepoint-matched control group, a large sample size, and comprehensive disease information at diagnosis. Compared with previous analyses of antibody repertoires in population-based cohorts such as the Lifelines study [23], the present design further enables evaluation of temporal antibody trajectories across multiple pre-diagnostic timepoints and allows assessment of differential antibody signatures up to a decade before diagnosis. Equally important, this study demonstrates the feasibility of combining large pre-diagnostic biobanks with high-throughput serological profiling, a strategy that may also be applicable to the study of other immune-mediated conditions such as RA, lupus, or T1D. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply massively parallel serology at scale in a prediagnostic cohort, thereby establishing a potential framework for similar analyses in other biobank-linked diseases. Certain limitations of this study also warrant recognition. These include the relative uniqueness of our cohort consisting of active US military service. However, it should be noted that, due to its unique design, a comparable pre-diagnostic cohort like PREDICTS does not (yet) exist, which for now precluded external validation in an independent cohort. Our findings may have limited external generalizability with respect to the broader UC population, as the PREDICTS cohort predominantly consists of male participants (>85%) and elderly-onset IBD is underrepresented in this population. Although age and sex are known determinants of antibody epitope repertoires in population-level analyses, this demographic structure of PREDICTS precluded robust evaluation of age- or sex-specific effects. Furthermore, potential effects of initial treatment initiation around the time of diagnosis cannot be fully excluded, although considered highly unlikely as initiation of such treatment typically affects deployment and active duty status. Furthermore, potential effects of initial treatment initiation around the time of diagnosis cannot be fully excluded, although considered highly unlikely as initiation of such treatment typically affects deployment and active duty status. Another limitation is that detailed information on geographic location or seasonal timing of sample collection was not available within the DMSS-DoDSR. Although cases and controls were matched on the calendar year of the diagnostic timepoint to partially account for temporal effects, regional or seasonal differences in infectious exposures (which may influence antibody repertoires) could not be evaluated. Additionally, while our findings strongly suggest potential microbial and non-microbial triggers contributing to IBD pathogenesis, causal inference cannot be made without supportive mechanistic data. Finally, it is estimated that PhIP-Seq may only detect ~10% of the entire antigenic space [16,29], although there is no current technology that can effectively surpass the high-throughput potential of PhIP-Seq. While PhIP-Seq does not yet cover the full antigenic space, its breadth, scalability, and compatibility with archived serum samples make it uniquely suited for discovery efforts in large prospective biobanks. In summary, this study presents a novel resource of immunological information spanning a period of up to 10 years before IBD diagnosis, which highlights the vastness, diversity, and specificity of early immunological changes preceding IBD development. More broadly, our work illustrates how large-scale serology can be leveraged to decipher prodromal immune changes in IBD, thereby opening avenues for early detection and improved risk stratification in IBD. Key messages What is already known on this topic • The preclinical phase of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) remains poorly characterized, limiting opportunities for early disease detection. What this study adds • Antibody repertoires against 357,000 antigens were profiled longitudinally in the pre-clinical phase of IBD, revealing distinct antibody signatures up to 10 years before diagnosis, especially against Epstein-Barr virus and bacterial flagellins. How this study might affect research, practice or policy • These results provide novel insights into early immunological perturbations preceding IBD, highlighting dynamic antibacterial and antiviral antibody responses and supporting hypotheses of molecular mimicry and immune dysregulation as early events in disease pathogenesis. • By systematically mapping longitudinal antibody trajectories in the prediagnostic setting, this study offers a framework to investigate early pathogenic mechanisms and to refine future strategies for risk stratification in IBD. Abnormal composition of intestinal bacteria —“dysbiosis”— is characteristic of Crohn’s disease. Disease treatments include dietary changes and immunosuppressive anti-TNFα antibodies as well as ancillary antibiotic therapy but their effects on microbiota composition are undetermined. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, we analyzed fecal samples from a prospective cohort of pediatric Crohn’s disease patients starting therapy with enteral nutrition or anti-TNFα antibodies and reveal the full complement and dynamics of bacteria, fungi, archaea and viruses during treatment. Bacterial community membership was associated independently with intestinal inflammation, antibiotic use, and therapy. Antibiotic exposure was associated with increased dysbiosis, whereas dysbiosis decreased with reduced intestinal inflammation. Fungal proportions increased with disease and antibiotic use. Dietary therapy had independent and rapid effects on microbiota composition distinct from other stressor-induced changes and effectively reduced inflammation. These findings reveal that dysbiosis results from independent effects of inflammation, diet, and antibiotics and shed light on Crohn disease treatments. Graphical abstract INTRODUCTION The human gut microbiota is densely populated by microbes from all three domains of life together with their viruses (Hoffmann et al., 2013; Human Microbiome Project, 2012; Samuel et al., 2007). Crohn’s disease results from a pathologic interaction between the mucosal immune system and the environment, particularly the microbes residing in the gut lumen (Sartor, 2006, 2008) and is characterized by altered—or “dysbiotic”--gut bacterial composition (Huttenhower et al., 2014; Khor et al., 2011; Sartor, 2006, 2008). Numerous human genetic loci encoding proteins involved in host immune responses have been linked to Crohn’s disease (Jostins et al., 2012), but the impact of these genes on the dysbiosis associated with Crohn’s disease is limited (Knights et al., 2014). Rather, dysbiosis is hypothesized to be a response of the microbes, particularly bacteria, to environmental stressors such as the host inflammatory response (Huttenhower et al., 2014) and/or the Lewis et al. Dysbiosis is commonly characterized by an expansion of Proteobacteria and a decrease in Firmicutes, along with a decrease in community richness (Nagalingam and Lynch, 2012). Much less is known about the responses of other domains of microbial life to environmental stressors. Similarly, it is unknown whether dysbiosis resulting from inflammation is rapidly reversible. Patients with Crohn’s disease are exposed to antibiotics and dietary changes which are likely to affect the microbiota, but the influence of these factors and their interactions with each other are incompletely understood. Antibiotics are often used as an ancillary therapy for Crohn’s disease (Khan et al., 2011). However, the main therapies for Crohn’s disease includes episodic or chronic immunosuppression with corticosteroids, antimetabolite agents, or antibodies directed against host immune proteins such as tumor necrosis factor α (anti-TNF) (Borrelli et al., 2006; Grover et al., 2014; Rutgeerts et al., 2012). The anti-TNF medications are administered parenterally and are not expected to alter the gut microbiota composition directly. An alternative therapy, used predominantly in children, is the defined formula diet, also known as enteral nutrition therapy. Both elemental and polymeric formulae, containing, respectively, amino acids and intact protein, have proved efficacious in treating symptoms and intestinal inflammation in Crohn’s disease in addition to supporting nutritional needs for growth and weight maintenance (Borrelli et al., 2006; Grover et al., 2014). The efficacy of these diets is greatest when used as the exclusive source of nutrition(Grover et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2015). Dietary therapy has the advantage of avoiding immunosuppression but is difficult to maintain long term. If the mechanism of action of dietary-based therapies were understood, it might be possible to develop less restrictive diets that deliver the same therapeutic benefit. One hypothesis is that diet

If the mechanism of action of dietary-based therapies were understood, it might be possible to develop less restrictive diets that deliver the same therapeutic benefit. One hypothesis is that diet therapy alters the composition of the gut microbiota in a manner that contributes to the therapeutic benefit, though data supporting this are limited (Gerasimidis et al., 2014; Kaakoush et al., 2015). We reasoned that longitudinal characterization of the gut microbiome of pediatric Crohn’s disease patients initiating therapy would allow us to characterize the concurrent effects of intestinal inflammation, antibiotics, and diet on gut microbial community structure. We conducted a longitudinal study of 90 children with Crohn’s disease who were initiating treatment with either a defined formula diet or anti-TNF therapy, and compared them to 26 healthy control children. We tracked symptoms, mucosal inflammation, and changes in the gut microbiome over an eight-week study period. The gut microbiome was quantified using shotgun metagenomic DNA sequence analysis of longitudinal samples. Dysbiosis was quantified as the distance of each sample from the centroid of samples from healthy controls. Communities partitioned into two distinct clusters based on the bacterial composition, as seen previously (Frank et al., 2007; Gevers et al., 2014), one of which overlapped the healthy controls. The dysbiotic community was associated with increases in specific fungi, prior antibiotic therapy and higher concentration of human DNA in feces. By tracking the microbiota composition over the course of therapy, we found that dysbiosis was reduced in response to decreased bowel inflammation, and that inflammation, antibiotic exposure, and diet independently influenced different taxa. RESULTS Clinical outcomes in patients treated with a defined formula diet versus anti-TNF Ninety children initiated one of the study therapies (52 anti-TNF; 22 exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN); 16 partial enteral nutrition with ad lib diet (PEN)) (Supplemental methods and (Lee et al., 2015). EEN and PEN treated children consumed approximately 90% and 53% of daily calories from dietary formulas, respectively. Inflammation was quantified by measuring fecal calprotectin (FCP). Response to therapy was defined as a reduction of FCP to below 250mcg/g because this measure is associated with diminished mucosal inflammation (Lin et al., 2014). Reduction in FCP below 250 mcg/g was more common among those receiving anti-TNF (62%) and EEN (45%) than PEN (10%)(Lee et al., 2015). Microbial community patterns in Crohn’s disease and healthy controls Adequate stool samples were available from 86 individuals to conduct shotgun metagenomic analysis. Samples were collected at four time points: baseline, 1 week, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks into therapy (Table S1A). We also compared stool samples from 26 healthy children (Table 1) collected in a prior study (Wu et al., 2011), but analyzed by shotgun metagenomic sequencing here. None of the healthy children had received antibiotics in the prior 6 months. DNA was prepared from whole stool, and sequenced using the Illumina HiSeq paired-end method. After filtering out low quality, human and contaminating reads, we were left with 6.5×1011 bases of microbial DNA sequence for analysis. We quantified the bacterial taxonomic composition using MetaPhlAn (Segata et al., 2012). After filtering out very low abundance genera, comparison of median relative abundances showed 14 of 45 genera differed between children with Crohn’s disease and healthy controls (FDR controlled p (q)<0.05 by Wilcoxon rank sum test; Table S1B). The Crohn’s patients had reduced relative abundance of Prevotella, Eubacterium, Odoribacter, Akkermansia, Roseburia, Parabacteroides, Alistipes, Coprococcus, Dorea and Ruminococcus and increased abundance of Escherichia, Klebsiella, Enterococcus and Veillonella. Community patterns were analyzed using PAMK (partitioning around medoids with estimation of number of clusters) to find the optimal number of clusters, and visualized after multidimensional scaling (MDS) (Figure 1B). Thirty of 45 genera differed in abundance (q<0.05) between the two clusters (Table S1C). The far dysbiotic cluster was characterized by an increased relative abundance of Streptococcus, Klebsiella, Lactobacillus and reduced relative abundance of Faecalibacterium, Parabacteroides, Dorea, Blautia, Holdemania, Collinsella, Coprococcus, Odoribater, Prevotella, Bacteroides, Dialister, Eubacterium, Alistipes and Ruminococcus. The top five most predictive genera were Blautia, Faecalibacterium, Dialister, Lactobacillus and Bacteroides. Reduced diversity was observed in both clusters relative to healthy subjects, and in the dysbiotic far cluster compared to the near cluster (see Supplemental Results). An analysis using phylogenetic attributions at the species level yielded similar conclusions (Figure S1C and S1D). In summary, baseline samples clustered into two groups, with the far dysbiotic cluster being more distant from the healthy controls and characterized by altered bacterial composition and lower diversity. High levels of human DNA in stool correlated with dysbiosis In processing the metagenomic DNA from stool, we observed that the proportion of human DNA varied widely (Figure 1C). The percentage of human reads was low in the healthy controls (mean=0.87%, max=10.1%, minimum=0.05%) relative to patients with active Crohn’s disease (mean=16.6%, maximum=94.2%, minimum=0.01%; p<5×10−11), with over 50% of the sequence reads mapped to human in 49 Crohn’s disease samples. DISCUSSION Here we assess the concurrent effects of inflammation, diet, and antibiotic use on the the gut microbiome in pediatric Crohn’s disease. The environmental stresses experienced by Crohn’s disease patients were associated with changes in microbial taxonomy that mostly differed among the stressors studied (Figure 5). We observed that patients with Crohn’s disease can be categorized into two groups defined by the composition of the bacterial populations, paralleling previous studies based on 16S rRNA gene tag sequencing (Frank et al., 2007; Gevers et al., 2014; Tong et al., 2013). We further showed that dysbiosis involved differences in microbial gene representation, increases in fungal representation, and higher levels of human DNA in stool. Antibiotic exposure, which is common in this population, has also been identified as a risk factor for new onset Crohn’s disease (Card et al., 2004; Margolis et al., 2010) and was strongly associated with the dysbiosis observed here. further altered the composition of the gut microbiota, possibly due to elimination of regular table food, despite having a favorable effect on gut inflammation. By our definition, the effect of diet qualifies as dysbiosis, though we note that the changes were distinct from the other stressors studied (Figure 5). Finally, effective therapy with either anti-TNF or EEN reduced, but did not completely eliminate, the dysbiosis present at baseline. Thus our data demonstrate that diet, antibiotics and inflammation each independently influence different components of the microbial community. We described two clusters of patients based on microbiota composition, though the data can be characterized as either a continuum or a dichotomous grouping. The two clusters were associated with clinical features such as antibiotic use and human DNA, but did not appear to predict response to therapy. Thus, the biologic and clinical significance of the clusters remains to be determined. There were very few taxa whose abundance was associated with more than one stressor. However, the genus Alistipes was increased with EEN, but diminished by antibiotic treatment, raising the possibility that antibiotics antagonize the beneficial effects of EEN. The independent effects of antibiotics, diet and inflammation likely reflect different mechanisms. Antibiotics are direct toxins to bacteria and may facilitate outgrowth of fungi. Changes in diet provide novel substrates supporting bacterial growth. Inflammation may select for bacterial taxa able to live in the setting of oxidative stress. The normal oxygen gradient in the colon influences the composition of the gut microbiota with a higher abundance of Proteobacteria in the microaerobic environment of the mucosal surface (Albenberg et al., 2014). Disruption of the epithelium and bleeding due to active Crohn’s disease is expected to lead to greater intraluminal oxygen, which in turn would favor outgrowth of taxa belonging to the Proteobacteria phylum. Others have documented increased richness of fungi in patients with Crohn’s disease using older methods, but have not linked this directly to specific fungi, environmental stressors or linked changes in the bacterial microbiota (Ott et al., 2008; Richard et al., 2015). In a separate study using sequencing of fungal gene tags, we found that Cyberlindnera jadinii (also known as Pichia jadinii or Candida utilis) was proportionally increased in Crohn’s patients (Chehoud et al., 2015), confirming the detection of this lineage here. In this study four of the five fungi detected (Candida, Clavispora, Cyberlindnera, and Kluyveromyces) showed increased representation in Crohn’s disease samples at baseline in the absence of antiboitic use. Independently, antibiotic use was also associated with increased colonization by all five fungi. Diet therapy showed the opposite behavior--after one week, fungal colonization was diminished (Figure 5). Thus increased fungal colonization is associated independently with disease and antibiotic treatment, and diminished with EEN. The reduction with EEN may be a consequence of lower consumption of fungi in food (Saccharomyces and Cyberlindnera are both found in foods), or due to a change in the microbial environment in the gut with EEN, paralleling the change in bacteria. The importance for pathogenesis is unknown, though we note that antiSaccharomyces antibiodies are used as a biomarker in IBD (Peeters et al., 2001; Prideaux et al., 2012; Quinton et al., 1998), and fungi have shown to exacerbate colitis in mouse models (Iliev et al., 2012).
